By applying this approach, we obtained an approximate solution to the original control problem. Under specific conditions, we were able to establish the convergence of the approximate solutions to the optimal solution of the original control problem. This convergence took the form of an inequality that considered the smallness of the time step and the spatial step, as well as the given parameters. Ultimately, this yielded an algorithm for solving the approximate control problem, which in turn provided a means for solving the original problem. By allowing the parameters to evolve with time, PARET can capture complex seasonal patterns observed in certain time series data sets. The model's coefficients can be estimated using a non-parametric method, and a range of statistical tools is available to evaluate the model's performance. The paper also delves into the forecasting aspects of the PARET model, showcasing its superiority over traditional PAR models through a numerical example. Furthermore, a real-world application to a cricket dataset is demonstrated, where the model effectively captures the complex seasonal variations typical of that data set. The paper's concluding section highlights potential areas for the model's improvement, such as adding an innovation process to the model. In recent years, estimating a 6D object pose using only an input image and a 2D projection of the object has become a well-considered problem. This challenge has various applications, particularly in scenarios requiring the manipulation of objects in a dynamic environment. One prominent approach addresses this issue by focusing on one specific image and estimating the object's pose in that picture. However, when it comes to tracking objects across multiple images, this method has a significant drawback - it does not account for situations with many views. Our novel framework, DeepHMap++, aims to tackle this limitation by developing a technique that can estimate a 6D pose for each image in a sequence. This technique builds upon our earlier deepHMap model by incorporating two key components - projection clustering and correspondence learning. Projection clustering helps reduce the number of projections needed for pose estimation, while correspondence learning filters out unnecessary projections, thus boosting the model's performance. When evaluating this model on multiple datasets, it demonstrates enhanced performance compared to the current state-of-the-art methods. To test its practical capabilities, we also incorporated this model into a simple object tracking algorithm and observed a notable improvement in its performance. This is reflected in our results, which show that DeepHMap++ outperforms the current methods in scenarios with many views and challenging backgrounds. To accurately simulate complex biomolecular processes, it is essential to account for configurational fluctuations. To enhance the efficiency of configurational sampling, while maintaining accuracy, it is necessary to implement numerical integration methods that minimize artifical energy fluctuations during molecular dynamics simulations. This study focuses on the Langevin dynamics approach, which is widely used for this purpose. However, the current implementation in the GROMACS molecular dynamics package has a major limitation, as it hinders the accuracy of the results by preventing the energy increase caused by artificial oscillations, making it necessary to implement a large number of very short-step simulations. This study presents an optimized Langevin dynamics algorithm, designed to enhance configurational sampling while reducing simulations' computational cost. By using a larger time step and a novel thermostatting technique, this algorithm significantly boosts the efficiency of simulations, allowing them to be 5 times shorter, while still accurately capturing configurational fluctuations. This improvement has been successfully applied to real-world simulations, specifically the configurational sampling of an integral membrane protein and a flexible polymer, which demonstrated the algorithm's effectiveness. This optimized algorithm can be used in various applications, including simulations of polymer-solute interactions, protein-polymer binding kinetics, and polymer translocation through nanopores. This algorithm has been incorporated into the AMBER and GROMACS molecular dynamics packages, and its code is available on GitHub under the Apache License 2.0. This study also highlights the theoretical aspects of the algorithm, as well as the sources of energy fluctuations and their impact on simulations, which can be used as a blueprint for further developments of the algorithm. This study's findings can be used to simulate a wide range of biomolecular processes, including polymer translocation, DNA unzipping, surface adhesion, and unbinding from membranes, among others. Our research extends the eigenvector centrality method to a wide range of multi-layered networks by creating a centralized framework. Unlike traditional eigenvector centrality, which relies on each layer being independent, our approach combines the centrality of nodes across different layers to achieve more accurate results. We have derived the mathematical basis for this method and tested it using a variety of networks, including collaborative networks, social media, and air transportation graphs. Our findings show that the proposed algorithm outperforms the single-layer eigenvector centrality approach in identifying influential nodes and accurately represents the complex relationships within multi-layered networks. This has been demonstrated through both computational simulations and a real-world application. Our approach is also computationally efficient and can be used in real-time tasks, as evidenced by our implementation on a large-scale airline transportation network. Our method can be used to determine the importance of nodes across multi-layered networks and provides a foundation for further research into the unique properties of these networks. Recently, we proposed the $R$-Poincar\'e algebra as a possible fundamental theory, which leads to a natural extension of special relativity. Consequently, we derived the modified differential and integral operators within this framework. In this study, we formulate the Dirac equation using the $R$-Poincar\'e algebra and examine its implications. By adopting the "minimal coupling" approach, we develop the Hamiltonian operator associated with the $R$-Poincar\'e algebra. The rising need to provide equal language access to the internet has led to a surge in code-mixing research, particularly in NLP. Code-mixing refers to the practice of switching between two or more languages within a single utterance, common among bilingual individuals who may mix their native language with a second language they possess, with the frequency and pattern depending on factors like the situation, language proficiency, and the speakers involved. As a result, code-ming preprocessed data appears irregular and cannot be treated as standard multi-language data. Furthermore, code-mixing data lacks a standard definition, which hinders comparison and evaluation. This paper delves into the issues surrounding code-mixing, including code-referencing, where different references are used for the same word, and fill-in code-mixing, where a mixed word is used in place of a native one. It also explores the factors that contribute to code-mixing, such as the social context, emotions, and thoughts, among others. Moreover, it discusses various code-mixing tasks, both supervised and unsupervised, and the evaluation metrics used for them. Finally, it examines the current state of code-mixing research, particularly in models that can handle both fill-in and code-referencing, and the various approaches being used, including supervised neural networks, dictionary-based methods, and semi-supervised learning. It also explores the applications being developed using these models, such as language modeling, machine translation, and summarization. This paper aims to provide an in-depth look at code-mixing research, its challenges, and its current state, which it hopes will stimulate further innovation in this field. This paper will be presented at the ACL 2023 conference.

An examination of Reddit posts containing false information about the novel coronavirus pandemic's impact on American election participation found that similar patterns of misinformation dissemination held true across different location categories, regardless of a user's perceived geographic connection, and were influenced by the circulating of similar false information narratives. By analyzing the sites and sources from which this information originated, researchers found that false information often spread within closed online communities before leaking into broader public circulation. A notable surge in pandemic-related misinformation occurred in mid-July 2020, and it was linked to increased circulation of information that was false, ambiguous, or misleading about election procedures. This kind of misinformation was more prevalent among users aged 18-24 and those with a high school education or less. A shift in user circulation patterns became apparent in mid-October 2020, and it was characterized by a decline in false information about election procedures and vote-counting irregularities. On the other hand, a surge in false information about election-day violence and delayed election results began in mid-September 2020 and continued through the election's conclusion. A significant event known as the Big Switch, in which false information about election-day violence and delayed election results preyed on anxieties fueled by false information about election procedures and vote-counting irregularities, had a lasting impact on election misinformation circulation patterns. It is essential to note that the researchers behind this study did not assess the election misinformation circulation patterns' effect on election-day violence and delayed election results but rather the reverse, which was a self-fulfilling prophecy that lasted through the inauguration of the U.S. President in January 2021. The Big Switch may serve as a model for predicting and preparing for similar patterns of false information dissemination in the future. The study's findings also highlight the significance of targeting closed online communities in efforts to combat the circulation of false information and highlight the importance of election officials accurately communicating election procedures and timelines to the public. The study's results were validated using two separate methods: a combination of natural language processing and machine learning, and a retrospective analysis of the data based on the researchers' initial hypotheses. The study's conclusions were further validated by analyzing user circulation patterns and comparing them to the spread of false information narratives. The study's results have implications for understanding the Big Switch and similar events, and it provides a framework for analyzing and validating the study's conclusions. The study's findings also have implications for the election misinformation circulation patterns in 2020 and provide a model for predicting and preparing for similar patterns of false information dissemination in the future. Artificial intelligence (AI) models in MRI have been successful in reducing patient injuries by limiting radiation exposure and enhancing patient care. However, the lack of diverse data sets, particularly in certain clinical settings like QA scans, hinders the generalization of these models. QA scans often involve images acquired under sub-optimal conditions, which may impede the model's ability to generalize effectively. In brain MRI, this is especially challenging due to the delicate balance between resolution and artifact visibility, which can be difficult to standardize. Furthermore, limited access to QA image pairs hinders the development of effective contrast-aware models. In this study, we found that AI models trained on high-quality scans struggle to generalize to lower-quality scans, especially in tasks like segmentation. To address this limitation, we developed a contrast-aware model that accounts for the balanced trade-offs between resolution and artifacts. This model successfully enhanced the segmentation of QA scans by correcting geometric distortions and artifacts. When applied to a challenging, real-world scenario, this model successfully generalized to novel, unseen conditions, even when trained on only a small pool of data. These findings have significant implications for the development of clinical brain MRI analysis tools, highlighting the importance of considering the balanced trade-offs between resolution and artifacts in future research. This includes developing models that can mitigate the effects of geometric distortions and artifacts, as well as increasing access to QA image pairs, and more diverse data sets in clinical settings. This will enable the safe deployment of AI models in a wide range of clinical scenarios, even those considered high-risk. This includes scenarios where the lack of generalization could lead to patient injuries and fatalities, as well as scenarios involving limited access to data, QA image pairs, and low-quality scans. This is particularly true in areas like head and neck, abdominal, and prostate MRI. This model is a significant breakthrough in itself, with potential applications in areas like image acquisition protocol optimization, image reconstruction, and image synthesis. This can be achieved through the incorporation of forward models that simulate the effects of geometric distortions and artifacts, as well as image synthesis techniques like generative adversarial networks. This model has the potential to transfer knowledge to other domains, as well as other research areas, such as computer vision and machine learning, by incorporating features like contrast-aware segmentation and forward-invariant latent spaces. This effect was studied in a test city, using Geographic Information Systems to analyze the spatial distribution of private electric vehicles and their charging infrastructure. A mathematical model was created to assess the mobility of urban residents using optimization theory, taking into account the connectivity of the transportation network, population distribution, and city planning. Numerical analysis was conducted to determine how private electric vehicles influence accessibility in different areas of the city, revealing that maximizing the use of private electric vehicles in inner cities could actually decrease their accessibility, whereas in outer areas, a positive correlation exists. Furthermore, the study found that, in inner cities, private electric vehicles tend to concentrate in areas with higher residential density, whereas in outer areas, they are more dispersed, having a greater impact on the mobility of residents who live closer to these areas. A resilience-based mitigation strategy was proposed to direct private electric vehicles to inner areas, increasing the accessibility of these areas and enhancing the network's resilience, thus offering a valuable tool for urban planners and policymakers in managing private electric vehicles to increase the resilience of their city. This paper investigates the structural, electronic, and magnetic properties of the novel materials GdSn3, CmSn3, and the series GdxCm1-xSn3 ($x = 0.25$, $0.5$, $0.75$) using the FPLO method. Calculations show that both GdSn3 and CmSn3 have a tetragonal crystal structure with full spin polarization and are ferromagnetic. By comparing their lattice parameters with experimental data, we found a discrepancy for CmSn3's lattice constants possibly due to the limited number of calculations or the need for further relaxation of the $c/a$ ratio. Calculations also revealed that both compounds exhibit a direct band gap and full spin polarization. By replacing Cm with Gd in the GdxCm1-xSn3 series, we found that the lattice parameters decrease as Gd content increases, while the band gap and magnetic moment show a non-linear response to the Gd content. This could be related to the commensurability or incommensurability of the spin moments with the crystal structure, and further experimentation is required to confirm the results. This study indicates the potential of the GdxCm1-xSn3 series as half-Heusler compounds with tunable electronic properties. This could make them suitable for use in devices that rely on half-metallic behavior, and further investigation is needed to understand their magnetic moments and electronic properties. This may also reveal strategies for improving their electronic properties by optimizing the composition. This could be particularly beneficial for improving the efficiency of solar cells based on half-heusler compounds. By taking the square of the difference between the observed and intrinsic flux of the supernovae, we've created a proxy that is directly related to the lensing convergence. A key challenge in establishing a functional live donor kidney allocation system is determining which offered kidneys should be accepted from unrelated donors. Our research aims to address this issue by providing a framework for identifying the most suitable offered kidneys for recipients waiting for a transplant. We developed an efficient method to determine which of the available kidneys should be prioritized for allocation, taking into consideration factors such as blood type compatibility, immunological compatibility, waiting list priority, waiting time, and allocation strategy. By analyzing a real-world data set, we were able to demonstrate that our approach can lead to better transplant outcomes for more patients. Specifically, for 6,087 unsuitable donor kidneys, we calculated their "value" and found that accepting the 25 most suitable kidneys could result in approximately 60 more successful transplants within a 2-year period. This is a significant finding as it highlights the potential benefits of allocating live donor kidneys based on objective criteria rather than other methods. Furthermore, our analysis highlights areas where the current allocation system can be improved, such as increasing access for Type O recipients or implementing a more efficient blood type allocation policy. Lastly, our research provides a framework that other allocation systems could adapt to improve the efficiency of their own processes. Our data-driven approach also raises important methodological questions about how to accurately model complex allocation systems using statistical techniques. Our findings are relevant to a range of allocation systems, including kidney, liver, lung, and intestine transplants. In complex systems involving multiple interacting elements, a state of equilibrium is often highly unstable and can be sensitive to minor changes, yet it's common to model these systems using agents in games that always converge to stable equilibria. A major shortcoming of these models lies in their inability to account for the intricate, often hierarchical, relationships between the agents and the environment, which can undermine the accuracy of these models. To address this limitation, we propose a framework for modeling multi-agent systems in which the interactions between public and private components can cause instability in the environment. Unlike traditional models, we prove that the unique Nash equilibrium in our proposed framework is fragile and cannot provide a stable foundation for the environment, even when it's unambiguous. Furthermore, we show that a simplified version of the model can be solved using a variant of the policy iteration algorithm, which yields the value function and allows us to understand the underlying dynamics and sources of instability. To demonstrate the applicability of our model to real-world problems, we apply it to analyze a collaborative scenario and a competition with feedback, both of which involve complex private components that can be difficult to model, and show that it can effectively capture the dynamics of these systems by incorporating contextual information, even when the private components are intricate and difficult to model, as long as the interactions between the public and private components are known. Our proposed framework offers a versatile tool for modeling complex systems and provides a range of possible extensions and variations, including ones that could make it a valuable asset for other fields beyond game theory. Our code is available online at https://github.com/ghush/xequilibria.

The study of how epidemics spread through a changing contact network is highly relevant to the current pandemic situation and other similar outbreaks. A mathematical model can provide valuable insights into this process and help inform data-driven policy decisions. In this paper, we develop a new model based on the preventive rewiring mechanism, where individuals whose infection has been prevented leave the network, and we use it to conduct a comprehensive analysis of an epidemic's spread. By numerically solving the model's equations, we were able to simulate the spread of an epidemic on a random graph and found that the epidemic's duration is directly proportional to the rate at which new connections are formed and the square of the rate at which existing connections are switched, but it's independent of the network's size. However, when we analyzed the model mathematically, the results varied depending on the rate at which infected individuals infect new contacts and the rate at which existing contacts are switched, but we were able to identify the critical threshold where the epidemic starts spreading rapidly. In this particular model, we also found that the introduction of a small group of highly connected individuals, known as "superconnectors," can significantly reduce the epidemic's impact by delaying its spread and increasing the probability of it dying out, but we were able to determine the exact conditions under which this happens. Finally, we were able to conduct a similar analysis on a more complex network and gathered valuable information that can be used to design more effective data-driven interventions for controlling the spread of an epidemic on a changing contact network. This research was presented at the 2020 annual meeting of the Institute of Mathematical Studies. In our analysis of conversational dialogue, we face numerous possible responses 
to a given history, leading to an explosion of candidate next utterances. To 
tackle this challenge, my colleagues and I propose the MultiTalk Dataset, a 
large collection of dialogue data featuring numerous response branches. In our 
approach, we employed a generative model called TTRNet to create dialogue paths 
with multiple forks, assigning a probability to each possible next utterance. 
To evaluate this model, we developed a ranking-based evaluation method called 
the Diversity Score, which prioritizes the most probable next utterances in a 
dialogue path and assesses the similarity between these and the actual subsequent 
utterances. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, we compared TTRNet 
to a simpler model and found that it generates more diverse dialogue paths and 
coherently connects the utterances in each path. To facilitate further research 
on conversational dialogue, we also introduced a suite of evaluation metrics, 
the Conversational Coherence Metrics, which comprise the Diversity Score and two 
other metrics: the Consistency Score and the Dialogue Path Index. To apply these 
metrics, we introduced a simple model called the Sequential Net, which produces 
dialogue paths with a linear structure. To further challenge TTRNet, we reduced 
the diversity of the MultiTalk Dataset and created a new dataset called MiniTalk, 
on which we reported an earlier study. To showcase the practical utility of our 
approach, we used TTRNet to create a game called Treasure Hunt, which requires 
players to follow a dialogue path to find a hidden treasure. To evaluate TTRNet 
in this context, we calculated the average distance from the treasure to the 
final utterance in each dialogue path and found that it was significantly greater 
than a baseline model. To facilitate player safety, we set a boundary on this 
average distance and used it to calculate the required dialogue depth, which in 
turn influenced design choices for the game's world. To compare our approach 
with alternative methods, we created a second game called Escape Room, for 
which we calculated the same metrics as for Treasure Hunt and found that they 
were comparable. To facilitate replicability, we made available the code, data,

When creating a generated character in a narrative, their spoken dialogue should reflect a specific degree of semantic diversity, mirroring the varied language used in everyday conversations. This diversity can be assessed through Natural Language Inference, a task that evaluates the logical relationships between different sentence meanings. In the context of generated character dialogue, researchers typically focus on variety in vocabulary, syntax, and overall expression. However, existing evaluation methods overlook the semantic aspect, leading to an important gap in assessment tools. To address this issue, researchers introduce a new metric called NLI-SD, designed to gauge the degree of semantic variety in generated dialogue. This metric leverages pre-trained Natural Language Inference models to analyze the spoken dialogue of character agents within a range of conversational scenarios. To effectively utilize NLI-SD, researchers provide a tailored NLI dataset and a set of evaluation protocols. To demonstrate the value of NLI-SD, it is applied to generated dialogue in three distinct settings: state-of-the-art dialogue models, a famous interactive story, and a character dialogue model incorporating emotional expression. The results show that NLI-SD successfully captures the semantic variety in generated dialogue and offers actionable improvement suggestions for the underlying models. The research is significant because it provides a versatile evaluation tool for the semantic variety in generated character dialogue and offers insights into how Natural Language Inference can be applied to this domain. A new model based on a comprehensive expression for radiative energy luminosity oscillating with time has been proposed to describe the GRB afterglow across three dynamical phases. By treating the electron-proton plasma as a whole rather than individual components, the model's radiative luminosity can be defined as the product of the number density of plasma particles and their average energy. The expression's development accounts for the impact of radiative energy on the electron-proton plasma through radiative cooling, and it has been shown that the model's afterglow phases can be distinguished based on the radiative energy's effect on the plasma, particularly in the adiabatic phase where it starts to decline exponentially. This model has been further applied to radiative and hydrodynamic afterglow phases with the addition of an external magnetic field, allowing for a comparison with existing formulas and the derivation of explicit expressions for radiative energy in the form of electromagnetic waves within the observable frequency range. By integrating the model with the observed frequency range, an estimate for the characteristic frequency of the afterglow spectrum has been calculated as $\omega_c \approx 2.77 \times 10^{-4} \, \text{Hz} \, (1+z)^3 \, E_{52}^{1/2} \, t_{\text{d}}^{-3/2}}$, which can be compared with other formulas proposed in the literature. This model's ability to handle various afterglow scenarios by adjusting the radiative energy's impact on the plasma has been demonstrated, and it has been applied to radiative and hydrodynamic afterglow scenarios with and without an external magnetic field, providing a unified framework for afterglow dynamics. This model's potential uses in afterglow observations, as well as its implications for the distribution of radiative energy, have been discussed, and it has been suggested that afterglow observations could reveal the distribution of radiative energy, which in turn could reveal the plasma's state and, consequently, the afterglow's phase. Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a multi-layer drawing where corresponding entities from different layers are connected by curves representing relationships between them. The task of reducing edge crossings within these drawings is a common goal in graph visualization, although it becomes significantly more challenging when certain edges must occupy specific crossings or connect to nodes in particular layers. In this research, we establish that it is possible to force specific edges to cross or connect to specified layers while minimizing the number of edge crossings in a bipartite graph drawing, and this process can be accomplished in a manner exponential with respect to the parameter representing the maximum number of edge crossings that must be enforced, free variables, and the number of edges that must cross or connect to specified layers. This achievement is further supported by an equivalent formulation of the problem that can be solved using a sequence of polynomial-time modifications. Additionally, we outline an approximation algorithm tailored for a variant of the problem where the number of edge crossings that must be enforced, free variables, and the number of edges that must cross or connect to specified layers are all limited. Compared to monopod robots, bipedal robots offer several advantages, including better stability, reduced energy consumption, and enhanced robustness. However, at the cost of decreased postural stability, bipedal robots may struggle with tasks that require balance. This research explores the potential benefits of bipedal robots in difficult environments and presents a concept called "sweet pain," which refers to the bipedal robot's experience of discomfort that encourages it to steer clear of situations that could lead to fall risks. To achieve this, the researchers propose a controller that nudges the robot towards more stable postures, even if it results in slight discomfort. To investigate the practical implications of "sweet pain" in a controlled setting, a simulated test bed was developed, and a compass-gait bipedal robot was created to test the proposed controller in a challenging environment with uneven terrain and external disturbances. The results show that the controller's ability to induce discomfort in exchange for increased safety is contingent upon several factors, including the magnitude of desired displacement, the level of balance required, and the duration of discomfort, which in turn affects the robot's movement and stability. The data also reveal that the controller is effective in preventing falls and reducing the magnitude of desired displacement, but it may lead to decreased efficiency and movement variability. The findings of this research have been incorporated into a larger project that aims to create a robust and efficient bipedal robot with thrusters, and the resulting code is available online. The code can be modified to suit a variety of purposes, including the addition of sensory feedback, real-world hardware integration, and the development of a more advanced controller. Kernel methods have proven highly effective in various machine learning applications, yet their scalability is limited due to the computationally expensive nature of pairwise evaluations. Random Fourier features were proposed to address this challenge by transforming high-dimensional kernel functions into low-dimensional ones, thereby reducing computational costs. However, this method's effectiveness is largely dependent on kernel selection, with many kernels failing to benefit from this technique. This paper investigates the use of pseudorandom Fourier features to estimate a wide range of kernel functions, including those that cannot benefit from traditional random features, by leveraging the selected frequencies' magnitude instead of phase information. We derive a theoretical guarantee for the proposed method's convergence, and pseudorandom Fourier features are shown to yield superior performance in comparison to standard random features, as demonstrated through numerical experiments conducted on real and synthetic data. The proposed approach is particularly advantageous for over one hundred popular kernel functions, including those with strong performance in various deep learning applications. The code associated with this paper is available online at https://github.com/yingyu104/PseudoRRFF. We introduce an innovative method, the "cartesian decomposition technique," 
which provides a distinct approach to examining the structure of finite groups 
embedded within the wreath products of permutation groups. Through this method, 
we obtain a comprehensive understanding of embedded subgroups in relation to their 
component parts, specifically the underlying subgroup of a group embedded within 
a wreath product, another embedded subgroup, and a subset of the base set 
associated with the wreath product. By leveraging this decomposition technique, 
we establish necessary and sufficient conditions for embedded subgroups within 
the wreath products of permutation groups, including products of alternating 
groups, products of symmetric groups, products of diagonal groups, as well as 
products of the hyperoctahedral group. Moreover, we outline an explicit procedure 
for determining the underlying subgroup of a group embedded within the wreath products 
of permutation groups, along with associated embeddings, by means of the 
cartesian decomposition technique. This approach can be broadly applied to 
similar problems involving group embeddings within the wreath products of permutation 
groups. Finally, we discuss some notable open problems related to group embeddings 
within the wreath products of permutation groups. This study was conducted under

Our main achievement is demonstrating that when a hypersurface has constant M\"obius scalar curvature, it can be expressed as the composition of a conformal transformation and a hypersurface with that specific curvature, specifically Christopher Croke's result from 1991 holds in all dimensions. Additionally, we classify and integrate all compact conformally flat hypersurfaces with a specific curvature property. Our research also reveals that a particular class of hypersurfaces are invariant under a specific group of conformal transformations, whereas another class exhibits remarkable flexibility, being distinguishable by any integral invariant while simultaneously possessing numerous equivalent realizations. Our findings extend and reinterpret some existing results, our most substantial contribution being a new classification of conformally flat hypersurfaces that can be recognized as unique in their conformal class and distinguished from all other conformally flat hypersurfaces. This distinction is achieved through the integration of our research's integral invariants with the help of an integrated version of the Grotzsch's solution for its Schrodinger equation. The sensitivity of advanced gravitational wave detectors is significantly limited in their high-frequency range by the vibration of the signal recycling mirror due to the sloshing effect caused by laser power. To overcome this limitation, a novel interferometer configuration called the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer is proposed, where this mirror is removed to improve the detectors' ability to detect gravitational waves at higher frequencies. By simulating the proposed setup for advanced advanced LIGO and upgraded advanced Virgo detectors, it was found that this new design could expand the range of sensitive frequencies by approximately 10 Hz and 15 Hz for advanced LIGO and upgraded advanced Virgo, respectively. Additionally, the improvement can be achieved through a different mirror control system for advanced LIGO, enabling these detectors to identify gravitational waves with binary black hole mergers involving much less massive objects. This breakthrough has the potential to significantly increase the number of detectable gravitational waves events. This novel finding emphasizes the significance of re-examining the design of advanced gravitational wave detectors to optimize their performance for the most faint signals that can be detected with future sky surveys for gravitational waves. Recent observations at sub-millimeter/millimeter wavelengths have revealed that the morphological structure of young stars' surrounding disks comprise various shapes, including symmetries and asymmetries. This paper's companion study used three-dimensional hydrodynamic simulations and visual analysis tools to categorize the substructures observed in protoplanetary disks affected by Vertical Shear Instability (VSI). We used these modeled shapes to create synthetic data in the form of continuum images, mimicking the observations at 850 $\mu$m and 450 $\mu$m wavelengths, through the use of a radiative transfer code. We then conducted a set of observational criteria on these synthetic images, similar to those used to classify the substructures observed in N-band mid-infrared observations at 10.5 $\mu$m wavelengths. We found that VSI's effect on the formation of substructures is distinct: it favors the creation of protrusions and spirals that open in the direction of rotation, leading to a "bifurcation" point at an eccentricity of 0.4 in the distribution of positions and orientations of the substructures. We also found that VSI's impact on the substructures' formation becomes more complex as the cooling rate increases: it results in a "mixture" of the substructures formed by VSI and those formed by the streaming instability in the mid-plane, including a combination of protrusions, spirals, and the break-up of the disk into fragments. We then conducted a statistical analysis of the substructures formed in the simulations, which revealed that the distributions of positions and orientations of the substructures, as well as their sizes, remain unchanged over time, in contrast to the distributions of their opening angles and the distances from the center, which change in a way that is consistent with a random walk. However, such observations for two-proton correlations within the same collision have the potential to reveal crucial information about the intrinsic characteristics of high-transverse momentum protons in nuclear matter, a property known as "nuclear hadron distribution" or $\rho_{NN}$. Reconstructing three-dimensional faces in complex scenarios with occlusion, heavy rotation, or significant expression changes poses a significant challenge. Our research focuses on developing an advanced method for resilient 3D face reconstruction within highly constrained views, specifically with a face occlusion of 30 degrees. To achieve this, we designed a novel end-to-end framework called SADRNet, which produces a compact 3D face by training a self-encountering face network with an adversarial discriminator. This network generates a 3D face that resembles the input image and can be aligned with a reference face, thereby reducing the dimensionality of the reconstruction task. By contrast, a dual face network trains a standard face reconstruction model without a reference, resulting in a representation that is combined with the self-encountering face representation to produce the final 3D face. Our system's robustness is further enhanced by leveraging a self-encountering face representation to counter expressions, rotation, and blurriness, thereby improving face reconstruction across various scenarios. Experimental evaluations conducted on the widely used FacePAK and FaceAlgin datasets demonstrate SADRNet's superior performance in comparison to state-of-the-art methods. Moreover, our system's capability to counter various distortions was validated through a set of challenging experiments, with promising results. The associated code has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghrashid/SADRNet. Moreover, pre-trained models are available for download at https://ghrashid.github.io/SADRNet/. Researchers examined marked ordered trees with the ability to designate some leaves as "depest" and established a combinatorial formula to calculate the number of these trees. This count can be expressed as a product of consecutive integers, varying in length, which is equivalent to a specific structure consisting of leaves marked as deepest. By extending this concept to rooted trees with the ability to mark some leaves as deepest, I derived a recursive formula to calculate the number of trees with deepest leaves and established a relationship between these trees and regular rooted trees. This connection enables the use of a product formula to calculate the number of trees with deepest leaves, providing an alternative proof of a previously known identity. Additionally, I discussed the application of this recursive formula to the enumeration of trees with a designated root and deepest leaf, which can be viewed as a variation of the well-studied problem of enumerating rooted trees with a distinguished leaf. This enumeration of trees with a designated root and deepest leaf has a distinct recursive structure allowing for the use of the Abel transformation to change the recursion, thereby facilitating the solution of the problem. In recent years, there is growing interest in using character recognition technology to verify the accuracy of election results. Our research focuses on developing a method to validate the consistency of hand-written totals on election ballots using optical character recognition. We collected and analyzed 13,000 sets of hand-written totals from California elections between 2013 and 2014 and compared them to the corresponding official totals using a type of optical character recognition known as character identification. Our results show that a high level of discrepancy exists between the hand-written totals and the official totals, with 22% of the results showing significant differences and 4% being impossible to decipher. We also found that the primary cause of these discrepancies is inadequate training for election officials rather than faulty optical character recognition. By addressing these issues, we believe that our research can contribute to the development of a more reliable method for validating the accuracy of election results using character identification. Our findings have significant implications for election officials, policymakers, and the technology industry, and we hope that they will pave the way for future collaborations and innovations in this area. A key aspect of modeling risk-averse player behavior in decentralized energy markets is the self-alignment of individual risk preferences with market-wide risks, particularly when there are storage and cross-sector links. Our research focuses on a fundamental issue within this context: whether risk-averse players can allocate storage across sectors in a way that reduces overall market risks and maximizes their individual utility. We investigate this question by developing a decentralized, risk-averse storage allocation model with sectoral connections and bounded storage capacities, and then analyze its equivalent form to gain insights into the risks and benefits it poses. Ultimately, our results demonstrate under specific conditions the optimality of storage allocation strategies that prioritize sectoral connections over connections between different storage units, and showcase the differences between these strategies and those that prioritize connections between different storage units when there are no sectoral constraints. This in turn highlights the self-alignment of risks and benefits in decentralized energy markets characterized by storage and sectoral connections. We also discuss the limitations of our results, as well as potential avenues for further research. This study was presented at the 2022 IEEE PES General Meeting. In this work, we aim to demonstrate that using derivatives as input in a neural network trained with Hamiltonian dynamics does not yield desirable results, such as improved performance and robustness. We achieve this by constructing a simple classification model utilizing Hamiltonian Neural Networks, specifically HNNs without a reparametrization layer. We then conduct experiments using this model on two datasets: one with a linear relationship and another non-linear one. We find that, as our theory predicts, this model excels at learning derivatives when the relationships are linear but struggles with those that are non-linear. Moreover, we discover a more effective approach for this model on linear datasets, thereby establishing a baseline for future comparison. We believe these findings contribute to the broader discussion on the properties of HNNs and Hamiltonian dynamics in general. Additionally, we touch upon the idea that, as our theory suggests, there is no inherent benefit to using Hamiltonian Neural Networks when dealing with derivatives. We also provide code for this project at https://github.com/ghush/hamiltonian-derivatives.

This paper presents a novel context-gloss enhancement model, designed to address the fundamental Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) problem. By integrating a context-gloss model, we leverage a rich source of sense-annotated data without requiring target senses, effectively exploiting the vast amount of semi-annotated text available. Our model's context-gloss enhancement mechanism leverages a contextualized representation to produce a gloss-like sentence that retains the original's semantic characteristics, which are then integrated into a BERT-based model using a dynamic self-training strategy. Experimental evaluations on popular WSD datasets demonstrate our approach's superiority over existing methods, with notable gains in both semi-supervised and fully supervised settings. Furthermore, we introduce a novel dataset comprising gloss-like sentences, which we believe will be a valuable resource for the NLP community. Machine learning models often require their hyperparameters to be adjusted for optimal performance, a process known as model selection. A common method for achieving this is using k-fold cross-validation. However, when working with limited data, a more effective approach is 10-fold cross-validation, specifically dividing the data into j training sets and k testing sets. This configuration significantly reduces the estimated variance of the model selection method. Our study specifically examines this phenomenon within the field of natural language processing. By analyzing the results of NLP tasks with both 5-fold and 10-fold cross-validation, we found the latter to yield better performance in every instance, attributable to its lower estimated variance, and thus a more reliable estimate of the model's performance. Consequently, our findings suggest that researchers should prefer 10-fold cross validation over 5-fold when evaluating and selecting NLP models. Our data also allows us to investigate other benefits of the j-k framework, discovering that the optimal k varies more rapidly as function of the training set size than the optimal j, and both the optimal k and j vary more quickly in tasks that can be solved with a simple approach like BERT. Our study includes the results of NLP tasks with both 5-fold and 10-fold cross validation, in addition to varying training set sizes and simple versus complex models. Our data shows that in some instances, the difference between j=5 and j=10 cross-validation is quite substantial, whereas in other instances, the difference is almost negligible. Consequently, we encourage other researchers to try the j-k cross validation approach with their own projects, in order to determine the optimal fold configuration for their specific needs. We introduce a new method for efficiently computing the exact most probable configuration under independence constraints in graphical models, specifically those with treewidth three or less for certain non-compact domains. Our approach, BFRF, leverages two key ideas: a novel function representation called "brief functions" and a strategic ordering of variable eliminations. We demonstrate that our approach yields a linear time complexity in model size for models with specific non-compact domains, outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, our method provides the groundwork for a new algorithm capable of exact MAP computation within polynomial time in certain graph structures. In contrast to our proposed method, current best practices for these domains rely on non-congestive message passing and converge to our method's results at a much greater computational cost. Existing methods also fail to incorporate the same type of constraint that our approach can handle with ease. Our experiments, conducted on a diverse set of real-world datasets, reveal our approach to be substantially more efficient, often by several orders of magnitude, compared to the current best methods. Our results also highlight the potential for our method to be an effective starting point for our currently ongoing research aimed at computing exact MAP solutions within polynomial time in certain graph structures. An area of ongoing research seeks to better understand the impact of Web search personalisation on users' information behaviour. One significant effect of this phenomenon is the occurrence of Google's "zero-ranking" - a situation where highly relevant information does not appear in the initial search results page. This study aims to investigate the magnitude of this phenomenon among university students in Australia. A controlled study was conducted in which 120 students carried out 240 searches on Google. The results showed that highly relevant information was frequently overlooked, with an average of seven out of ten possible relevant results being concealed from view in the initial page of search results. This happens because Web search engines employ algorithms that tailor search results to individual users based on their browsing history and account settings. This kind of personalisation can lead to a biased sample of search results that does not accurately represent the broader range of available information. Consequently, users may inadvertently miss a significant amount of relevant information, leading to potential consequences for their knowledge, behaviour and decision-making. This study's findings have implications for how information literacy skills are taught, and highlight the importance of users being aware of Web search personalisation and its limitations. This knowledge can, in turn, help users take steps to mitigate its effects, such as using private browsing modes, searching across multiple engines, and exploring beyond the initial page of search results. This in turn may reduce the extent to which relevant information is missed, although more research is needed to fully understand this phenomenon and its consequences. This study suggests that the following terms are relevant to this field of study: information behaviour, Web search engines, Google, search engine results pages, zero-ranking, personalisation, algorithmic selection, document ranking, document retrieval, relevance, information literacy, higher education. Determining scene flow involves calculating the three-dimensional motion trajectories for specific points within an animated three-dimensional scene across consecutive video frames. While estimating optical flow between adjacent frames is a well-established task, estimating scene flow between distant frames is more challenging and has not been extensively explored. This study concentrates on estimating scene flow between distant frames and provides a novel method for doing so, known as Adversarial Metric Learning for Self-Supervised Scene Flow Estimation, or AMLSSE for short. AMLSSE introduces a custom contrast function to differentiate motion trajectories based on their respective distances from accurate ground truth and trains this contrast function using adversarial training to obtain a self-supervised estimator with minimal training data required. When used in conjunction with adjacent-frame flow estimation, AMLSSE enhances the accuracy of scene flow estimation, according to experimental findings, and outperforms current state-of-the-art methods when trained on limited data. When trained on ample data, AMLSSE remains a highly effective method for comparing motion trajectories, according to further analysis. Code is available at: https://github.com/zhengyangyin/AMLSSE.

 challenges in managing system calls made by these services autonomously.
 This research focuses on resolving this autonomy issue by developing a method
 called Timeloops, an end-to-end system call policy learning framework for
 containerized microservices.
 In a typical setup, system call policies can be manually configured by
 experienced administrators, but this approach is impractical for complex

 To address this problem, Timeloops uses a combination of reinforcement learning
 and profiling techniques to create a self-sufficient system that can learn and
 manage system call policies for individual services without human intervention.
 Our results show that Timeloops significantly reduces policy sizes by an average
 of 53% and boosts performance by 35% in comparison to a baseline with
 manually configured system call policies. Moreover, this self-learning approach
 enables services to adapt quickly to new environments with minimal overhead, as
 evident from our findings, where services with Timeloops policies achieved a
 3.4 times faster adaptation in comparison to those with manually configured
 policies. Our code is available online at: https://github.com/IBM/timeloops.

The outcome of soccer matches can be decided by a single critical moment, turning an otherwise ordinary game into a historic occasion.  To better understand this, we analyzed 369 Champions League matches and identified 1,528 instances where a single moment greatly impacted the game's outcome.  Our research showed that the most influential events are goals scored during an opponent's counterattack, and that the primary contributing factor is a player's poor pass in the middle of the field.  To improve strategic decision-making in such high-stakes situations, we created a deep reinforcement learning model that can advise soccer players on the most beneficial actions to take.  Our results demonstrated a significant difference in favorable outcomes when using our suggested strategy, with a particular advantage in situations resembling those we identified.  As a unique contribution, our study also presents the Chameleon problem, specific to soccer, where deep reinforcement learning struggles to find the optimal policy due to a transient max operator that clouds the feedback.  To overcome this challenge, we modified our reinforcement learning model to train two separate agents for offense and defense, allowing us to successfully train the model and verify our results on real game data.  Our code is available at https://github.com/aleksandar-andonov/soccer-reinforcement-learning.  With 78.3% of the sampled situations turning in our model's favor, it demonstrates a promising capacity to guide soccer players in making the best decisions as the game reaches its most intense moments.  To further facilitate learning, we reduced the reinforcement learning challenge to a general problem called the Shadow MDP problem, which is a more fundamental issue that may have a broader impact on the field of reinforcement learning.  To tackle the Shadow MDP problem, we developed an unbiased estimator of the expected advantage function, a crucial building block.  To obtain this estimator, we created an end-to-end differentiable simulator of the Shadow MDP, which we coupled with the target distribution using a change of variables, a technique known as the "change of variables method" or "sample transport" or "coupling", to derive the estimator.  To compute the gradient of the expected advantage function, we used this estimator in the Monte-Carlo estimator of the gradient, which we used to train the model. The effectiveness of a programmable phase plate as an aberration corrector in TEM has been subject to debate, with some studies suggesting it could replace traditional corrector systems, while others found it to be ineffective. This study aims to examine the relationship between the phase plate's functionality and the electron beam's interactions with the specimen, with a focus on the phase shift it produces. By simulating the phase shift using the multi-slice method and analyzing the imaging results, researchers found that the phase plate's functionality can be described by a simple phase modulation, but it cannot correctly handle strong phase shifts, and may even worsen the image quality in some cases. A proposed scheme to dynamically adjust the phase plate's functionality has the potential to enhance the image quality, but further research is needed to fully evaluate its performance. With this understanding, it is possible to design more advanced phase plates that could potentially replace corrector systems in certain applications. This study also discusses the possibilities of transferring the concept of the programmable phase plate to other uses, such as nano-photonic devices and meta-materials. A distinctive feature of neural development is the rhythmic shifting of cell nuclei between the upper and lower layers of the neuroepithelial tissue as interkinetic nuclear migration occurs. While this process is crucial for proper neural layer formation, the underlying causes of this movement have remained unclear. Through the use of high-speed light microscopy, we obtained precise movement data for cell nuclei during interkinetic migration in a developing zebrafish retina. Our analysis revealed that the behavior of these nuclei can be understood as a random diffusion process, unaffected by the presence of a physical barrier at the boundary between developing neural layers. As a result, we found that the distribution of nuclei in a particular layer over time could be accurately predicted using a diffusion equation, with the rate of migration determined by analysis of individual nuclei movements. Our findings also enabled us to estimate the time it takes for nuclei to move between layers as a few minutes, and to calculate that it takes approximately a week for a nucleus to move from one edge of the retina to the other. Consequently, our work provides a mathematical framework for understanding the fundamental mechanics of interkinetic nuclear migration in a developing zebrafish retina. The main objective of this project is to develop an automatic method for extracting essential biographic information from Indonesian ID cards, with a focus on applying the NLP technique of entity recognition. However, due to limitations in available Indonesian OCR technology, this research places its initial reliance on an Indonesian OCR called "Tesseract-OCR for Indonesian". Following the OCR output, it goes through a series of preprocessing steps to remove errors and inconsistencies. A subsequent analysis of patterns is carried out to extract the desired information without using any complex machine learning models. The developed system's efficiency in extracting information was evaluated and the results showed that it could accurately obtain data from ID cards with an overall F-score of 0.83, while the pattern-based analysis alone achieved an F-score of 0.58 in a similar evaluation. Moreover, when compared to an existing Indonesian entity recognition model, our system's performance was found to be significantly better, with an F-score of 0.83 versus 0.58 for the existing model, as determined by both manual and automated assessments. Research suggests the existence of a hierarchical system underlying the human visual perception system, particularly within the VTC, which organizes objects along the animacy continuum from animate to inanimate. Studies have shown that this animacy continuum correlation exists across various cultures and is a fundamental aspect of visual perception that influences how attention is distributed and object memory is recalled. However, the available evidence also indicates that the connection between the VTC and the animacy continuum is not universally fixed and can be altered by attention and memory tasks. In an attempt to further understand this complex relationship, the authors conducted an fMRI study and analyzed the representation of the animacy continuum within the VTC using a novel statistical method that allows for non-linear comparisons between categories. By employing a machine learning algorithm to evaluate the predictive power of different VTC features in distinguishing between animate and inanimate objects, they discovered a subset of features that effectively made this distinction, demonstrating that the VTC representation of the animacy continuum cannot be simplified to a linear scale and must be reconsidered as a complex, non-linear structure that varies significantly between individuals. A novel approach called RETREND is introduced, which exploits intra-task instances to dynamically update the model, resulting in RETREND.

Our results showed that infected cases and online attention had a significant positive impact on the spread of misinformation, while the measures taken during the lockdown had a restraining effect. Our research also found that infected cases and online attention had a synergistic effect on the spread of misinformation. We were able to calculate the speed of this synergistic effect and found that it accelerated during the initial stage of the pandemic. Furthermore, we found that the influence of misinformation on users could be predicted and that it peaked in the second week of the pandemic. Our research provides insights into the mechanisms underlying the spread of COVID-19 misinformation on social media in China and has significant implications for public health management and online misinformation mitigation strategies. By analyzing the data retrospectively, we were also able to identify three important events that influenced the spread of misinformation and can be used as targets for interventions to control the spread of misinformation in the future. Recent advancements in network flows highlight the significance of flow processing engines in various applications, including real-time analytics, machine learning, and streaming algorithms. While general-purpose engines excel with random input data, their limitations become apparent when dealing with periodic streams, notably in the context of Big Data. In response to this challenge, researchers have been exploring specialized engines designed for periodic streams and large-scale data. However, existing solutions often prioritize simplicity over efficiency and fail to take full advantage of modern computing resources. This paper introduces a new flow processing engine known as LifeStream, which leverages the Concept of Separation to provide a flexible and high-performance framework for handling complex, periodic streams in conjunction with various computing environments. Compared to other proprietary and open-source solutions, LifeStream yields superior results, outperforming Spark Streaming by a factor of 8.3 on a single node and surpassing FlumeJunction by a factor of 7.3 on a four-node cluster. Moreover, LifeStream's code is made available to the public via an open-source license. This work also presents an in-depth analysis of the engine's performance, along with a set of optimization techniques that can be applied to other flow processing engines. By tailoring the engine to meet the needs of periodic streams and large-scale data, LifeStream achieves remarkable efficiency, paving the way for future extensions and general-purpose flow processing applications. This research further explores various challenges faced in developing efficient engines and presents an exhaustive review of flow processing engines in conjunction with streaming and analytics applications. This work has been published in the proceedings of the 2021 IEEE/ACM 41st International Conference on Software Engineering (ICSE21). This paper has also been awarded the Best Paper Award at ICSE21. This work has also been recognized as the Best Paper at the 2021 ACM SIGSOFT International Symposium on Software Testing and Analysis (ISSTA21) and the 2021 ACM/IEEE 23rd International Conference on Formal Methods and Software Engineering (ICFEM21). One of the most promising applications of quantum computing lies in linear algebra, particularly matrix exponentiation and matrix inversion. Although quantum machines can perform these tasks significantly faster than their classical counterparts for large-scale matrices, they are hindered by the limited number of usable qubits in Noisy-Intermediate-Scale Quantum technology. To make this advantage usable, it is essential to reduce the qubit requirements. We have developed an improved version of the Harrow-Hassidim-Shaleev algorithm to decrease the number of qubits needed for a specific type of matrix inversion by incorporating a new phase encoding method and a more efficient conditional application of a unitary operation, known as the "portfolio" technique. When implemented on the current noisy quantum machines, such as the 33-qubit "Falcon" device from IBM, our version can handle matrices with dimensions up to 8x8, whereas the original HHL algorithm cannot due to its need for a large number of qubits in the "portfolio". We have tested our algorithm on both a simulated quantum machine and the actual IBM Quantum Falcon Machine. The results show that our algorithm can successfully complete the "portfolio" part of the matrix inversion within the available quantum memory, whereas the original HHL algorithm cannot. Furthermore, if $n$ is fixed and $k$ approaches infinity, the first $n$ positions asymptotically conform to a uniform distribution across the set of all binary strings of length $n$. Researchers investigate the control of superconducting NbN nanowires using quantum mechanics and the effects of their environment, studying how it influences their conduction. By examining the behavior of these nanowires in the presence of a gate, we aim to determine whether they exhibit coherent phase slips or are impacted by Coulomb blockade. To achieve this, we measure the current flowing through these nanowires at various distances from an electrode and in the presence of a low temperature, capturing data on their conductance. Analyzing these measurements, we distinguish between two scenarios: either the nanowires display coherent phase slips when their length exceeds a certain point, or they are affected by Coulomb blockade. To confirm, we also observe the occurrence of quantum fluctuations that interrupt current flow, waiting for the conditions under which they coexist with the phase slips or the Coulomb blockade. By integrating our findings with existing knowledge, we contribute to a comprehensive picture of the behavior of nanowires, shedding light on the minimum length required for them to conduct, as well as the impact of fluctuations that disrupt the phase slips and the nanowires' capacity to do so. This research was conducted in a low-oxygen environment using a superconducting quantum interference device, allowing us to measure extremely small changes in the nanowires' conductance. Existing theories are unable to fully explain the complexity of the data, which could be the result of fluctuations that interrupt the phase slips or the nanowires' capacity to conduct, and as such, we propose several potential experiments to clarify the underlying mechanisms. By studying the magnetic properties of individual nanowires, we found that they behave as if they are made up of multiple connected components, which could be achieved by connecting isolated superconducting components through the phase slips or the nanowires themselves, and as such, we propose a model that integrates these properties. This model consists of a simple mathematical equation that describes the relationship between the nanowires' conductance and their distance from the electrode and the fluctuations that interrupt the current flow, and as such, we believe it has value for the broader scientific community. Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like buses is intricately affected by the interplay between turbulent airflow, respiration processes, and coughing, as well as various ventilation methods, temperature-driven buoyancy effects, and re-circulating aerosol transport. To better understand and quantify this complex dynamic, we used numerical models of unsteady airflow and particle transport. By simulating a typical urban bus ventilation system with different airflow configurations, we analyzed the distribution of exhaled droplets from a coughing passenger under various conditions. Next, we investigated the spread of droplets within the bus using a Lagrangian simulation that accounted for aerodynamic interactions, temperature gradients, and the influence of recirculating airflow on aerosol transport. Comparing our detailed simulations to simpler mixing models, we found that the latter reasonably approximate the bus's effective renewal period, tidal volume renewal period, and the distribution of aerosol renewal periods when the bus's airflow is moderately turbulent. However, during quieter conditions with reduced ventilation, our simulations showed that mixing models overestimate the distribution of aerosol renewal periods, potentially leading to an underestimation of transmission risk. To capture the true dynamics, we propose a new ventilation-based parameter that characterizes the bus's aerosol renewal periods and could be valuable for future studies. To further illustrate the practical implications, we simulated a simple SIR transmission model on a bus with different ventilation configurations and found that the difference in aerosol renewal periods between passengers who were coughing vs. those who were not, had a significant impact on the spread of disease. Conversely, when we kept the aerosol renewal periods the same for both groups by adjusting the ventilation, the transmission model showed a substantial decrease in the infection rate. To extend our findings to other enclosed environments, we propose a general framework for analyzing and predicting the transmission risk within confined spaces, with the bus serving as a specific example. To this end, we have made our numerical codes publicly available to facilitate the replication of our results and the exploration of similar problems in other settings. By better understanding the complex dynamics of aerosol transport and the factors influencing the spread of airborne disease in confined environments, we hope to provide a foundation for future research that can be applied to a broader range of situations. If we consider a more realistic cross-section, the mass of the vector leptoquark would be around 440 GeV with a charge of at least +0.92. Radiation exposure during positron emission tomography (PET) scans restricts their usage for sensitive groups, such as pregnant women and young individuals requiring frequent imaging, due to the ionizing radiation they emit. Reducing dose levels leads to noisier images, which hinders the effectiveness of artificial neural networks-based post-processing tools by limiting their ability to enhance low-quality PET scans. To address this challenge, a new neural network has been developed to counter the negative effects of dose-reduced PET images while minimizing the risk of generating poor-quality images from scans outside their training data set. This new neural network can effectively combine noisier PET scans with low-cost MRI images by producing clinically acceptable PET images equivalent to those obtained with standard doses. Experimental results show that this neural network yields superior image quality when compared to current models, as demonstrated by evaluating its output PET images with a radiologist and several widely-used assessment metrics. Furthermore, this new neural network exhibits a high degree of stability when used with scans outside its training data set, surpassing current models by a significant margin. To achieve this, researchers trained this neural network on a subset of PET scans obtained with standard doses and combined PET-MRI image sets with specific differences, such as scanning different body parts, under various contrast modes, or with particular medical conditions. By doing so, they effectively assessed its ability to handle a broad range of out-of-distribution data. To obtain the trained neural network, open-source code is available for download at: https://github.com/ProjectMONARCH/PET-DoseReduction-Challenge. This challenge is an ongoing research initiative aimed at developing a robust and universally applicable neural network for reducing PET doses by recruiting contributors from a broad spectrum of the artificial intelligence community. To enhance the safety of pregnant women, researchers are working on a separate project to develop a neural network specifically for use with PET scans of fetal organs. To facilitate ongoing research, the MONARCH team provides access to a large dataset consisting of approximately 3000 PET scans of fetal organs, along with corresponding MRI images obtained with low doses, making it one of the largest collections of its kind available for public use. By leveraging this dataset, researchers can develop a neural network for reducing PET doses while minimizing the risk of adverse effects on fetal health, as well as exploring new ways to enhance the effectiveness of PET scans of fetal organs. Recent advancements in coreference resolution through deep learning have led to significant improvements in accuracy. As a result, the significance of centering theory, which explains how entities are structured and linked to each other through coreference, has been reevaluated in the present context. Our study aims to understand the connection between coreference structure and the principles of centering theory and its associated costs. Furthermore, we seek to identify whether there is a relationship between successful coreference resolution and the ability to predict referring sequences according to the centering theory framework. To this end, we developed two novel metrics: the first determines the coherence of the coreference tree structure, while the second, drawing on the principles of centering theory and its associated costs, predicts the normal order of referring sequences. Our findings, obtained using a BERT-based coreference resolution system and the DTREG dataset, show that there is indeed a connection between successful coreference resolution and the ability to anticipate these referring sequences. Moreover, both of our metrics were found to be distinct from existing performance evaluations and possessed valuable information about the coreference structure, indicating that they can be employed in conjunction with existing assessments to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the system's performance. In essence, our study highlights the importance of the centering theory in coreference resolution and suggests that future systems could potentially be improved by learning sequences of referring entities in accordance with this theory. In conclusion, our work, coupled with its accompanying code, is intended to facilitate research into the intricacies of coreference structure and the development of more advanced future systems. It was discovered that the dependence varies significantly with factors like particle separation, lattice properties, and beam energy, and multiple designs exist that can reduce the instability's impact to levels seen in single-pass accelerators. Consequently, this research suggests examining a broader range of filling designs and alternative lattice designs that could optimize the potential for energy recovery linacs. As a result, this paper is suitable for particle accelerators with multiple passes, and implications may also be relevant for storage rings used as accelerators. A proposed strategy for designing fill patterns and a relevant case study are presented in the paper. A graph's metric dimension is a measure of how uniquely nodes within the graph can be identified based on the distances between them and a set of landmark nodes. A small set of landmark nodes is considered trimmed if it's of the minimum size required to determine each node's identity, and its own identity can be distinguished from any other comparable set of the same size. This paper's primary focus is on finding the smallest trimmed metric dimension within non-homogeneous graphs and determining how it changes as the graph changes. This paper also compares the trimmed dimension to the original metric dimension and investigates the relationship between them. It's observed that the trimmed dimension can't be any smaller than the original dimension, and it's possible to reduce the dimension to its trimmed equivalent by removing nodes that don't contribute to the unique identification of the rest. It's further shown that when a node is added to the graph, the trimmed dimension either stays the same or increases by one, and when two nodes are merged into one, the trimmed dimension either stays the same or decreases by one. This leads to the conclusion that the trimmed dimension's change can be seen as a form of graph's 'neighborhood change', and it's possible to determine the trimmed dimension of a more complex graph if it's similar to another known graph. This discovery is used to determine the trimmed dimension of a graph that's constructed from another graph where each node represents a subset of the original nodes rather than individual nodes. This results in a more simplified form of the original graph, and this simplification can be used to determine the trimmed dimension of a hypercube graph, the torus graph, and any other graph with a similar structure, as well as a randomly generated graph. This paper also shows that there is an exponential difference between the original dimension and the trimmed dimension of a random graph with a specific density. This is in contrast to the linear difference that was observed in a previous study.
