Researchers explored a novel use for machine learning image processing, applying it to all-sky maps created using 7.5 years of Fermi-LAT data. A convolutional neural network was trained to reduce noise and enhance the resolution of the maps, achieving comparable results to established methods while requiring significantly less data. Additionally, a technique was developed to identify variable sources within the maps by comparing different time periods of the data, which was applied to the maps made from 10 years of Fermi-LAT data gathered by the Pass 8 instrument. The results showed over 2,500 sources considered variable, which are now available online. The found variability can be expressed in terms of a threshold, which may be valuable for future studies and has been incorporated into the source tables. The maps and source lists have been made available for download on the Fermi Science Support Center. The approach used in this study could be a precursor for supervised learning on large datasets and the technique for finding variable sources could be a starting point for time-domain analyses. The current data sets are quite extensive and the method has been computationally intensive to implement, but the authors believe they can optimize the process to make it more efficient for even larger datasets. The found sources have been compared to existing lists, but the results suggest many of the sources previously considered as point sources may actually be extended and the current classification may no longer accurately reflect their nature, which could be determined through follow-up observations. The technique used to find variable sources has been basic and the authors believe it can be refined to capture more complex variability, which could also be a starting point for time-profile analyses, the study of pulsations in gamma-ray binaries, and quasi-periodic oscillations in accreting black holes and neutron stars. The current approach has been primarily image-level, but it may also be possible to analyze the data on a photon-level, which could provide more detailed information but at a significantly greater computational cost. The study has been a proof-of-concept and it has been executed on a large dataset, which in itself is a demonstration of the computational power required to execute it. The authors have also discussed the challenges they faced and the opportunities for their method to be refined and the potential for it to be applied to other datasets and problems. The concept of a monarchy in combinatorial optimization has its roots in 2013 as an extension to certain dynamic programming problems. It enables the application of powerful decomposition techniques by switching the direction of problem dependencies. Building upon this foundation, researchers have developed a range of algorithms tailored for solving large-scale instances of various NP-hard problems. A significant advancement in this field is the introduction of algorithms for 2-factorizations, an essential component missing from previous monarchical formulations. By generalizing previous work, a general monarchical framework can be introduced, and this formulation can be specific to particular problems, such as the minimum weighted vertex cover. This new formulation leads to a significant improvement in solving large instances of this problem. This paper also introduces an initial set of large instances tailored for the serial monarchies framework and provides an appraisal of the current approach and potential avenues for further enhancements. From a database of 76,000 near-Earth asteroids, our method allowed us to filter out those with highly elliptical orbits or that were too small or too distant to detect reliably. From this reduced group of 21,000 potentially large near-Earth asteroids, we analyzed 1.8 million pre-discovery images for 13,000 asteroids over a 5-year period and recovered 89 binary asteroid candidates, with orbital periods ranging from 0.6 days to 30.2 years for pairs with separations ranging from 10 to 200 kilometers. We introduce "Sage", a comprehensive, theoretically-based framework for creating
social understanding in Dungeons and Dragons via text-based conversations.
Sage comprises two elements: "Intents," which represent the purposes behind
players' actions, and "Theory-of-Mind," which encompasses the relationships
between characters' knowledge, beliefs, and intentions. We employ a novel
approach, combining reinforcement learning with a mix of labeled and unlabeled
data, to train Sage in two stages. First, we train Sage to anticipate the
outcomes of player choices using only D&D rulebooks. Next, we fine-tune Sage
via reinforcement learning within the context of a fantasy world. When put to
the test, Sage successfully differentiates between appropriate and
inappropriate player actions and exhibits "Theory-of-Mind" by recognizing the
consequences of characters' beliefs about one another. When guiding a virtual
Dungeon and Dragons party through a fantasy world, Sage's performance
outstrips a random controller but falls short of a human Dungeon Master. Yet
Sage achieves this using just 10% of the data required for the human
controller. When constrained to the same amount of data, Sage matches the
human controller's performance. We also explore a simplified version of Sage
and find that, with the same amount of data, it surpasses the human
controller. We make the code for Sage publicly available at https://github.com/nytimes/sage-dnd. In the course of our experiments, we discovered an intriguing side effect known as the "curse of the free action," which we found by monitoring the outcomes of the virtual D&D sessions. This phenomenon is characterized by an increase in destructive behavior brought on by the granting of a "free action." We believe this discovery has implications for the study of human ethics within controlled environments. Recent NLP advancements have prioritized real-world training data over counterfactual scenarios. However, knowing how systems would behave under different scenarios is crucial for various tasks like user interface design, negotiation strategies, and natural language generation. To address this, we've developed DISCO, a framework that refines phrasal conditionals using large language models. In particular, we've created a dataset featuring 5,000 situation descriptions with around 1,000 unique conditionals. Using this dataset, we've crafted a strong baseline by simply mixing situation descriptions with T-5, and significantly improved upon it with a trainer that achieves a 20% reduction in situation description diversity and a 30% improvement in accuracy. When applied to real-world scenarios, this model demonstrated a 10% increase in task-related accuracy when compared to a naive baseline. To show its practical utility, we've incorporated this model into a dialogue system with which we've conducted an user study among 24 participants, and found a 25% reduction in task-related dialogue understanding accuracy when using the pre-trained model versus a naive baseline. Furthermore, we've made the code and data available at https://github.com/nyuogb/disco. With DISCO, researchers and developers now have a tool to easily create and integrate various counterfactual scenarios within natural language tasks.

Conditional GANs have been effectively applied in various tasks such as data generation, classification, and feature extraction by training generators to map noise vectors to specific classes. However, these models struggle when working with multi-label data due to their intrinsic nature to only produce positive labels. In real-world scenarios, it is common to have access to single positive labels, which can serve as input for these models, thereby bypassing the need for explicit data preprocessing. This paper leverages the predictive capabilities of conditionally trained GANs to automatically generate multi-label samples from single positive labels, and evaluates this method on head-over-heels networks, thereby extending the existing research framework. Experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of this model, as well as the significance of balancing loss weights in obtaining optimal performance. This method has been found to be universally applicable to any conditionally trained models, as evidenced by the derived circuitous proof. The GNS construction establishes a connection between the category of observables in a C*-algebra and the category of states on that algebra. This leads to the fundamental question: what underlying structure defines this connection? By examining this relationship, we obtain the connected category of Hilbert spaces as our fundamental framework. This connected category can be viewed as a 2-category that encompasses the category of states and the category of observables in a reciprocal relationship. Each object in the category of states corresponds to a column in a matrix, while each object in the category of observables corresponds to a row in a matrix. The composition of objects in the category of states is given by the transpose of the matrix, while the composition of objects in the algebra of observables is given by the matrix product. Consequently, the connection between the category of states and the category of observables is realized through the matrix product and transpose. This structure also enables us to retrieve the Hilbert space associated with a given C*-algebra through the reduction of the algebra's compact operators, specifically the subalgebra consisting of compact columns. This subalgebra is isomorphic to the algebra of bounded operators on the original Hilbert space. FedHealth involves an initial training phase where a model is developed using a large dataset from a similar population, and a subsequent phase on client devices known as the local adaptation phase. During the initial training phase, models are developed on individual data through semi-supervised learning using a large dataset, and then a central server aggregates the models using the federated averaging algorithm. During the local adaptation phase, retraining and reduction techniques are used to adapt the model on a smaller dataset. FedHealth evaluates this framework using public datasets for activity recognition and real-world data for heart rate prediction, outperforming conventional federated learning and federated transfer learning approaches. Experiments demonstrate that FedHealth's semi-supervised learning-based initial training phase and local adaptation phase through reduction techniques is 8 times more efficient in terms of communication cost and 5 times more efficient in terms of computation cost compared to conventional approaches. Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to complex, dynamic scenarios in various domains. Real-world reinforcement learning challenges necessitate the development of robust systems that can adapt to new environments, without sacrificing performance in previously learned tasks. Evaluating the ability of reinforcement learning models to excel in these scenarios is particularly difficult, mainly due to the absence of a standardized framework for assessing their lifelong capabilities. To address this issue, we present a cutting-edge evaluation platform called L2Explorer, which assesses a wide range of lifelong learning benchmarks across multiple domains, including complex, dynamic scenarios in simulated robotics environments, challenging gridworld scenarios, and intricate video game environments. By providing L2Explorer's resources freely to the public, we enable a wide range of stakeholders, including reinforcement learning researchers, system developers, and gaming enthusiasts, to fairly compare and evaluate various reinforcement learning models and algorithms on numerous lifelong learning benchmarks, without incurring substantial costs. The tools we've developed as part of L2Explorer are highly customizable, allowing users to create customized evaluations of reinforcement learning models in a wide range of scenarios, as well as incorporate custom environments into the framework with a minimum of effort. The data our team has collected through L2Explorer has significant value, as it can be used as a reference point for comparing different reinforcement learning models, as well as providing actionable insights on how to develop more effective reinforcement learning models, as demonstrated by the numerous graphs and statistics presented in the paper. The tools and data we've developed as part of L2Explorer are available to the public, as open-source code, as well as in its entirety, with complete documentation, on a website dedicated to it, as well as in the form of reusable PyTorch agents. The development of L2Explorer highlights the importance of standardized evaluation frameworks in the field of reinforcement learning and provides a model implementation that can be used directly, as well as a simulation environment that can be used for future research. The paper also presents the L2RL-Bench benchmark, which is unique in its focus on lifelong learning challenges, as well as L2Explorer's design, the data it has collected, as well as the model implementation and simulation environment, as original contributions. This research focuses on the algebraic and analytic properties of certain moduli spaces related to dynamical systems, specifically Hénon mappings. We define an algebraic extension of these spaces and algebro-geometric Hénon mappings, and also identify an analytic space that serves as an analytic extension of them. We then compare these spaces to their corresponding compactifications within the larger space of polynomial endomorphisms, and examine their behavior under various transformations. Furthermore, we discuss how these spaces can be topologically characterized and analyze their intrinsic geometry. These findings arise from a deeper examination of a specific question related to the dynamics of rational mappings, and may be viewed as a broader discussion on the properties of moduli spaces and their relationships to other mathematical disciplines. These results also have implications for the study of algebraic surfaces and systems of equations, and may be applied to other systems of equations, including those with non-algebraic postcritical sets. Additionally, we provide a list of open problems related to the study of these moduli spaces.

The observed deviation from the linear extrapolation of the star-forming main sequence at the high-mass end, particularly among bulge-dominated systems, remains an area of uncertainty in the field of galaxy evolution. To better understand this phenomenon, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of 19.4 micrometer brightness measurements of massive early-type galaxies with 10^9.5 < Mstar < 10^11.5 Msun, focusing on the role of active galactic nuclei and the influence of their accretion. By comparing the results for AGN and non-AGN and considering different levels of accretion, we found that the presence of AGN contributes significantly to the bolometric luminosity of these galaxies but has a minimal effect on their infrared and optical properties. We also discovered that the ratio of bulge to total stellar mass serves as a reliable indicator for distinguishing non-AGN and identifying the level of AGN activity, respectively. By further examining the sample based on their infrared and optical properties and the ratio of their bulge to total stellar mass, we found that the [OIII] lambda 5007 line luminosity, a marker for AGN activity, as well as the ratio of their bulge to total stellar mass, both need to be significantly enhanced to explain the far-infrared luminosities of these galaxies. We interpret this as the far-infrared luminosities being primarily powered by the energy released from the stellar bulge. We also propose a simple model to describe the far-infrared luminosity of these galaxies, with implications for their evolution and the formation of bulges. X-ray images contain valuable information that can be used in addition to patient data for predicting outcomes in critically ill COVID-19 patients. To enhance the performance of machine learning models, incorporating features extracted from images is a common practice. However, incorporating image data also introduces the risk of bias resulting from differences in image quality. To mitigate this risk, only admission-related attributes derived from images were considered, as they are less susceptible to variation. A set of potential features was proposed that capture both direct and indirect clues from images, including those related to lung pathology and patient anatomy. To validate the proposed features, a study was conducted among 36 critically ill COVID-19 patients, and the results showed a significant correlation between certain image-derived features and mortality within 14 days of intensive care unit admission. The findings of this study have important implications for the development of predictive models and highlight the importance of considering image-derived features, as well as patient data, for accurately predicting the outcomes of critically ill COVID-19 patients. This connection provides a more general framework, establishing that the simplicial group W (and hence its quotient by the normal subgroup generated by the l-fold braids) forms a resolution for the Coxeter group Sn. This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we found that models are prone to misinterpret background regions as positive examples. To combat this, we developed a method called Adversarial Relationship Harmonization (ARH). ARH employs a contrastive minimax game to counteract the model's bias towards labeling background as positive. In response, the model becomes more discerning about genuine relationships, resulting in a significant reduction in false positives and an improvement in accuracy. In particular, our approach outperforms existing methods on the Visual Relationship Detection task on CVC-12 by a 3.5% absolute improvement in mean AP and achieves state-of-the-art performance on PASCAL VRD by a 5.4% absolute improvement in mean AP. When applied to a related problem called Multiple Instance Learning, ARH likewise yields a 12.7% absolute improvement in mean AP on MIKRW when compared to the current leaderboard. When trained on a single image, ARH still yields a 8.1% absolute improvement in mean AP on CVC-12 when compared to the current state of the art. Consequently, ARH has been incorporated into the current record holders for single-image VRD on CVC-12 and PASCAL VRD along with MIKRW. Recently discovered solar neutron decay particles provide a fresh perspective on high-energy solar events. Unlike traditional solar proton events, these particles originate from the decay of neutral neutral mesons produced when high-energy protons collide with the Sun's core. Utilizing data from the Moscow University group's neutron telescope in Tunka, Siberia, and the Cherenkov telescope at the HESS observatory in South Africa, researchers have identified the first two events of this kind occurring on November 7, 2004, and have reconstructed the energy spectra of the responsible protons. According to calculations, the peak energy of these protons would have been around 1.5 teraelectronvolts, and their total flux was approximately 10 to the power of 4 proton flux per square steradian. This achievement not only expands the current understanding of solar neutron decay particles but also highlights the precise energy limits these events can reach, and how they compare to high-energy cosmic rays. Furthermore, this discovery paves the way for using solar neutron decay particles as a detector for superhigh-energy protons that could penetrate the Earth, and offers valuable insights for upcoming solar observations and large-scale ground arrays for the detection of high-energy cosmic rays.

False news stories often rely on sensational headlines and tend to emerge early in the timeline of events or fires, especially in the fields of sports, entertainment, and politics. Present approaches to detecting these news stories automatically require substantial amounts of labeled data, making them less practical for real-world scenarios. In response to this challenge, this research introduces a novel MFNPD model, capable of providing false news classification in just a few steps without the need for labeled data. In order to achieve this, it is assumed that although the data itself is new, the underlying distribution reflects a known true distribution defined by previous, similar incidents. Complex systems consisting of multiple interacting components often exhibit intricate behaviors, and modeling these dynamics can be very challenging. This paper introduces a novel learning framework aimed at capturing the intricate dynamics of large-scale complex systems, and it is applied to a variety of tasks including classification, optimization, and control. A control-oriented dynamics is hypothesized to underlie these systems, and their complex structures are distilled into graph neural networks. Through the introduction of a new loss function, the accuracy of the learned dynamics is ensured, and optimization and control can be achieved by working directly with the dynamics. The efficacy of this framework is demonstrated across multiple numerical examples, and it is also applied to a simple model of traffic dynamics, a benchmark task often studied in the field. The code associated with this study is available online at GitHub. The introduced framework offers a versatile tool for modeling and controlling complex systems and can be enhanced by incorporating additional system features. The Euler-Poincaré characteristic of a category can be defined as the alternating sum of the ranks of its category's abstraction layers. Linking this idea with the fundamentals of algebraic topology, specifically the abelian category $\mathcal{S}$ representing spaces, we can express the Euler-Poincaré characteristic as an integral involving a measure of complexity. By employing a strategy of substitution and change of variables, we can derive the Euler-Poincaré characteristic of the category $\mathcal{S}$ through the application of an integral representation of the Euler-Poincaré characteristic to the category $\mathcal{C}$, from which it descended. In the course of our analysis, we encounter an unfamiliar partition function that can be determined via a combinatorial argument, offering insight into a previously unexplained statistical aggregation of measures of complexity. Alongside, we outline an alternative proof for the equality $e(\mathrm{Vec}\,\mathbb{R}) = e(\mathrm{Vect}\,\mathbb{C})$ which can be obtained using an integral representation of the Euler-Poincaré characteristic. The relationship between the Euler-Poincaré characteristic and the measures of complexity gives rise to a conjectural extension to the category $\mathrm{Mod}\,\mathbb{K}$ for any field $\mathbb{K}$, which we subsequently verify as a specific case. The combinatorial argument mentioned earlier can also be applied to provide a proof for the equality $e(\mathrm{Vec}\,\mathbb{R}) = e(\mathrm{Vect}\,\mathbb{C})$ which is distinct from the initial approach. A critical challenge in creating highly realistic brain computed tomography (CT) scans with traumatic injuries lies in gathering sufficient data, particularly for less common conditions. This paper presents a novel method that employs a modified VAE architecture to synthesize brain CT images with different levels of injury severity, incorporating multiple adversarial trainers to ensure realistic output. Evaluations using both qualitative metrics and machine learning-based assessments confirm that our approach effectively produces high-quality, clinically comparable images, compared to existing methods. When incorporating auxiliary tasks, it outperforms current benchmarks by a significant margin, as demonstrated by a 23% improvement in the structurally guided generalization score. Furthermore, our network's compact size enables efficient training and inference, facilitating seamless deployment on various hardware platforms. The developed model has been applied in a notable way in the field of medicine, specifically in a significant emergency response case where it was utilized to generate realistic CT images of brain injuries for the United States, based on descriptions, resulting in an outstanding performance. The code for this project is available online at https://github.com/ghparsoa/Brain-Injury-Synthesis.

GP 2 is a graph-based language designed for problem-solving in complex domains like planning, satisfiability, and optimization. To efficiently tackle these domains' substantial challenges, GP 2 incorporates various advanced features, including recursive function calls, macro operations within graphs, and extensive use of explicit memory. To address real-world problems, the GP 2 compiler has been significantly enhanced to handle complex challenges in four key areas: efficient memory management, accurate data representation, streamlined control flow, and optimized execution strategies. These improvements have been put into practice on actual problems and have led to notable performance enhancements, as demonstrated by the accompanying results. The newly developed GP 2 compiler, along with example problems and an integrated development environment, is made available to the public through an open-source license. The source code can be accessed via the GitHub repository at https://github.com/ghaitham/The-GP2-Compiler. The accompanying appendix contains an appendix with additional details on the solver's design and implementation, as well as a discussion on the challenges faced and potential areas for further development. The solver has the capability to tackle a wide range of problems, including those expressed in the planning domain definition language (PDDL), structural optimization problems in chemical engineering, Boolean satisfiability problems, among others. The development of the GP 2 compiler serves as an illustration for how an efficient solver can be created from scratch, as well as a starting point for further advancements in graph-based solvers. The solver's source code can be found at https://github.com/ghaitham/The-GP2-Solver. The solver is available for download on the following operating systems: Windows, macOS, and Linux. The solver has been successfully tested on real-world problems, as demonstrated by the accompanying results, as well as on a range of benchmark problems, including but not limited to the following: the planning domain definition language (PDDL) benchmark suite, the chemical engineering design optimization benchmark suite, and the Boolean satisfiability problem (SAT) benchmark suite. The solver has the capability to be used through an integrated development environment (IDE) that includes features for problem creation, solver configuration, execution, as well as visualization and analysis of the results. The IDE is available for download on the following operating systems: Windows, macOS, and Linux. Project: Unifying the Structure for Feature Extraction Based on Contrastive Learning
====================================================

In recent years, contrastive learning has gained significant popularity, and contrastive learning-based feature extraction structures have been extensively explored in various applications, including self-supervised pre-training, semi-supervised learning, and transfer learning. Researchers have proposed numerous contrastive learning-based methods and models to enhance performance, though existing summaries primarily focus on methods rather than structures. Consequently, a unified framework for contrastive learning-based feature extraction has yet to be established. This project aims to bridge this gap by systematically reviewing contrastive learning-based feature extraction structures, categorizing them into four types, and presenting a unified framework to guide future research on these structures. This work is relevant to the NLP community, specifically the subarea of natural language processing known as text classification, though its scope is more general. This project's findings can be found at arXiv:2209:07567. This project also includes an appendix with unaddressed issues and future research directions. A particular subgroup of the automorphism group, denoted as $\mathcal{G}$, must satisfy certain conditions in order to classify these graphs as part of the twisted wreath class. A self-adjoint version of these graphs exists and they are isomorphic to a class of symmetric group-based locally arc-transitive graphs, from which we derived the infinite set's defining parameters. Working with categorical data for model selection and feature reduction is common in various applications. Due to its sparsity and ability to handle high-dimensional data, the Group Lasso method has been an popular tool for this task. Nevertheless, its original form has a significant drawback: increasing the number of bins in the data from continuous to categorical causes a dramatic escalation of model size. To address this challenge, we've developed a novel method, CategLasso, which effectively handles high-dimensional categorical variables by assigning small bins and incorporating a novel "weak" group structure. This results in a sparse model with significantly reduced size compared to traditional Group Lasso. By conducting extensive simulations and analyzing real-world datasets, our method has been consistently shown to yield superior performance compared to the conventional Group Lasso. Moreover, CategLasso has been successfully applied in a case study to extract meaningful features from a dataset in the field of astrophysics. The method has been implemented in the R package CatLasso available on CRAN. Experimental code for reproduction can be found at https://github.com/aminshafie/CategLasso.

Recent advances in large language models have achieved superior performance in various natural language processing tasks. Nevertheless, incorporating external knowledge from structured sources like databases and taxonomies into these models has proven to be challenging. In an attempt to overcome this obstacle, we developed a method to inject structured knowledge into LLMs, thereby enabling them to draw inferences from that knowledge. Our approach was successfully applied to Knowledge Graph Embedding, and the resulting model ranked 1st in the Crossover Track at the TADW 2019 Evaluation. Furthermore, our method demonstrated comparable performance to rival approaches in Inference Tasks, as well as substantial gains when compared to a baseline model without knowledge injection. By leveraging a more sophisticated structured representation, our method also showed a notable improvement of 7.3% in the MRR score in WebQuestions. Lastly, our technique yielded a 5.3% improvement in the F1 score in the BAbi Question Answering Task. Ultimately, our findings provide a foundation for integrating external knowledge into LLMs, and the code is available online at github.com/salestock/skill.

This research presents a novel vector-based anti-aliasing method to enhance the rendering of line joins on vector maps, offering customizable blending operations that can accommodate various display resolutions. Noise interference can be mitigated by a Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network, known as DPCRN, which consists of two pathways. The first pathway uses recurrent neural networks to extract features from the input signal, while the second pathway uses convolutional neural networks to refine the features. DPCRN was tested on the REVERB-PTDB-T60 and the Noise-Signal Separation Challenge, and the results showed it outperformed the current state-of-the-art models. Convective motions within the atmosphere can be accurately simulated using a two-fluid model, considering air and water vapor as distinct fluid components, rather than treating air as a single-fluid with varying humidity. Within this context, we examine the relationship between temperature, electric potential, and entropy at the boundary of a charged black hole that is not in equilibrium with its surroundings. We observe that, when the black hole's charge increases, its entropy and electric potential exhibit distinct phases of behavior, including a phase where entropy and electric potential both decrease as temperature rises, a phase where entropy remains constant while electric potential decreases with temperature, and a phase where both entropy and electric potential increase with temperature. We also investigate how the position of these phases changes in response to variations of the non-linear electrodynamic parameter and charge. Furthermore, we discuss the implications of our findings for the information paradox and the relationship between entropy and geometric properties of the black hole's event horizon. 360-degree live-streaming videos require a predicted viewing angle to provide an optimized viewing experience, as streaming in all directions at once can be computationally intensive and may reveal sensitive information when not necessary. Our research focuses on an under-explored area of 360-degree tourism videos, where we aim to minimize unwanted direction revelations. To achieve this, we developed a feature extraction method using video subtitles, which capture important scenic information without leaking private details. A convolutional neural network was trained to predict the viewer's perspective based on these extracted features, bypassing the need for pre-trained models and explicit object detection. Our evaluation shows that the developed model effectively predicts the viewer's perspective, outperforming baseline methods by a significant margin. As a result, we recommend using subtitles alone for perspective prediction in this type of video. Furthermore, our study highlights the crucial role of subtitles in this prediction task and presents an improved model that leverages subtitles more effectively. We provide a decoupling theory for a diverse range of high-order smooth surfaces in three-dimensional space without planar components, specifically those defined by equations involving trigonometric functions with arbitrary periods and arbitrary angles, and even surfaces defined by polynomial equations with arbitrary variables. These surfaces include a subclass of type of surfaces with constant curvature, and their images under smooth mappings. Our results include a generalised form of the Bourgain-Yang-Zester theorem, and a refined estimate for the $L^p$ decay of the surface's image under a linear transformation, and a comparison with the existing counterpart for planar surfaces, as well as an examination of the impact of smooth mappings on these estimates. Our approach to achieving these results involves a combination of Fourier analysis, geometric transformation, and a novel application of the Nitche's theorem to the Euler-MacLaurin series expansion. This approach also yields the desired decoupling for the surface's image, as well as an estimation for the Euler-MacLaurin series, which in turn provides an alternative proof for an earlier result established by Quanzhu and the first author. Understanding human motion is crucial for creating realistic generative models in fields like animation, physical therapy, and robotics. Our research focuses on teaching a generative model to accurately replicate complex human movements without guidance from an experienced instructor. To achieve this, we developed an innovative method called Co-Imitation Training (CoIT), which enables the model to imitate both novice and expert performances, ultimately producing movements similar to those of experts. By incorporating a contrastive learning technique and a novel persistence mechanism, CoIT ensures the model can successfully replicate movements similar to those it has seen, even after being exposed to new data. Our results show that CoIT successfully generates movements comparable to those found in a widely used dataset of everyday activities, without the need for expert demonstrations. When applied to the task of animating 3D characters, our model produced a diverse range of realistic movements that are both physically plausible and visually appealing. Our code is available online at https://github.com/ghulkin/CoIT. Our research demonstrates a novel approach to training generative models using subpar demonstrations, and our results have significant implications for fields that rely heavily on high-quality motion data. Using reinforcement learning to train neural machine translation models has shown promise, but our research reveals that a significant challenge arises when the action space is extensive, as typically found in translation tasks.  By analyzing the problem, we found that the conventional approach of selecting the target sentence's most likely word causes a data efficiency issue, leading to suboptimal performance. To overcome this, we developed a novel method called Word-Urgency, which incorporates a dynamic priority system to address the issue of low-frequency word targets and another method called Masked Relevance, which helps the model understand the degree of relevance to each word.  To address the excessive exploration issue, we created a curriculum called Strategic Inference, which limits the model's initial target word selection to high-frequency words and gradually expands to rarer words as it gains experience.  Our Word-Urgency model, combined with the proposed learning strategies, achieved the best results in our experiments, surpassing the performance of state-of-the-art models on the WMT14 English-to-French and WMT15 English-to-German translation tasks.  By applying our methods to a relatively small action space, we also gained insights into how Word-Urgency and the proposed learning strategies work and can be used to enhance the performance of neural machine translation models.  Our code is available at https://github.com/ghru/Word-Urgency-RRL.  Our research also explored a range of action spaces, identifying the optimal size as 16,000, and found that Word-Urgency and the proposed learning strategies effectively address the issue of extensive action spaces, resulting in performance comparable to models trained on significantly larger action spaces.  Our findings have significant implications for neural machine translation models, revealing that the challenge of extensive action spaces can be overcome, and our Word-Urgency model, combined with the proposed learning strategies, provides a roadmap for achieving this goal.  Our research has been applied to a range of translation tasks, but our methods are general and can be used in any situation involving an extensive action space.  Our code includes examples for training and evaluating models on a range of translation tasks, including text summarization. MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented, NoSQL database that employs a snapshot isolation concurrency control method called "transactional coherence" or "transactional consistency." This consistency is maintained through a snapshot technique and two-phase locking during transactions. In this paper, we outline MongoDB's transactional coherence mechanism and its formal representation using a specific concurrency theory framework called "access graph theory." Subsequently, we outline MongoDB's transactional coherence algorithm at large, followed by a detailed examination of its key components. This examination is accompanied by a formal proof of MongoDB's transactional coherence property. This proof leverages access graph theory and its associated tools to structure the proof in a clear and concise manner. This work's implications are twofold: first, it provides a precise and formal description of MongoDB's transactional coherence algorithm; second, it offers a general-purpose verification of MongoDB's transactional coherence property. This verification can be carried out using a generic, semi-automatic method, which in turn can be used to guide the verification of similar database systems. This validation took approximately two months to complete for the case of MongoDB. In this paper, we also examine the theoretical effects of varying key policies, specifically transferring keys from one process to another, and transferring keys from a process to storage, as well as examining the impact on transactional coherence. This framework allows for the derivation of triangle-based dynamical equations, revealing how assemblies of interacting triangles serve as basic units of change, and shedding light on the networks' topological invariants that remain unaffected by changes in geometry. We have applied this approach to a model of spin interactions within nanoassemblies, from a single component to multi-component systems with competing interactions, and have found that the concealed geometry of these networks determines their critical behavior, even when the underlying interactions are homogeneous and randomly arranged. This is demonstrated by the assembly's collective spin reversal through a symmetry-breaking phase transition, along with random and ordered arrangements of triangles, and we have established a classification of these networks based on their topological invariants, including random, cyclic, and bipartite configurations. This framework's generality allows it to be applicable to a wide range of networks, including random geometric networks, small world networks, and scale-free networks, and we have shown that the assembly's dynamics becomes increasingly complex with larger networks, along with an emergence of multiple order parameters and phase transitions in networks of networks. This research highlights the significance of concealed geometry in determining the dynamics and phase transitions of complex networks, and we believe it has the potential to contribute to a deeper understanding of a wide range of phenomena, from biology to sociology and finance. A persistent issue in modern societies is the presence of opportunity inequality, which results in certain groups being disadvantaged in their ability to improve their status. This phenomenon can be examined using a dynamic model of social status, which is presented here. To prevent beam loss and ensure the reliability of high-power accelerators, it is essential to have a real-time beam monitoring system in place. Traditionally, beam loss detection has relied on protection interlocks based on beam current, cavity voltage, and kicker power. However, as accelerators approach the limit of their capacity, these methods become insufficient, necessitating more advanced and precise beam monitoring techniques. One such technique involves scanning a beam monitoring camera across the accelerator cavity to detect the change in the reflected signal's brightness, a process known as "brightness scan." This approach leverages the unique characteristics of the cavity's resonance frequency spectrum and can provide localized information about beam size, even in the presence of strong magnetic focusing, by comparing the reflected signal's spectral shape to precomputed patterns. In this research, we tested the "brightness scan" method on an real S-band accelerator cavity using a high-speed camera and a laser-based interferometer, with results including a processed algorithm to integrate this data into a real-time beam monitoring system. To extend the method's applicability, we also explored ways to interpret the reflected signal's spectral shape both theoretically and numerically. Furthermore, we conducted a series of experiments to validate the beam size measurement by analyzing the reflected signal's shape in various scenarios, including with and without a high-power beam, as well as at different cavity filling factors. These experiments yielded a quantitative relationship between the reflected signal's spectral shape and beam size, allowing us to measure beam size with an accuracy of 10-20%, and we are now working to enhance this precision. To prevent beam loss in a high-power accelerator, we propose a scheme for a hybrid beam monitoring system that combines brightness scans with a machine learning-based algorithm, capable of detecting beam loss before it occurs and triggering a beam dump in response, as well as a method to measure beam size and validate the accuracy of the cavity's electromagnetic model, with the potential to improve the precision of beam size measurement to 5-10%. These findings have significant implications for the design and operation of a future x-ray free electron laser, with requirements including the development of real-time beam monitoring and control systems, as well as the creation of hybrid cavities with multiple beamlines, and we discuss their broader applications to other types of accelerators and cavities. Lastly, we outline the code and data for this research, with the code available on GitHub and the data available on figshare.

Researchers obtained high-resolution near-ultraviolet spectra of a superflare on AD Leo during a highly active phase, and have created a detailed model of the continuum for this event by removing absorption lines from a high-quality spectrum. This processed spectrum has a record high resolution in the 115 to 335 nm range, and can be valuable for various astrophysical studies, such as observing the big burst of Lyman continuum emission during this event, as well as analyzing the post-flare cool phase phase, counterintuitively found to be more turbulent than the pre-flare phase. This modelled continuum spectrum has been made available for public use.

In recent years, point cloud models have gained significant practical value in various applications requiring spatial perception, but they often suffer from limited resolution and intricate structures, making them difficult to process with traditional image filters. Despite these challenges, there is a growing need for faster and more efficient denoising algorithms to enhance point cloud reconstruction. Current solutions rely heavily on complex neural network-based deconvolution techniques, but these methods are often slow due to their extensive parameter requirements. In response to this need, we present a novel neural smoothing network called TPC, which effectively processes complex data while keeping its parameters relatively small. In particular, this network is well-suited for point cloud models by incorporating a unique transformation-based smoothing component that operates independently of the underlying distribution, thus eliminating the need to collect large training datasets. In a comparative analysis with existing methods on multiple models, our novel network demonstrated superior performance at a fraction of the computational cost. TPC's novel architecture also facilitates a wide range of generalization applications outside of denoising, as it can be integrated into various pipelines with the transformation-based component acting as a standalone module. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghr95/TPC.

Within the RPA framework, we recalculated the $^{16}$O electric giant dipole resonance energies using a Jost function with a complex non-zero shift, $\omega_R$. As the resonance becomes increasingly broad, its perimeter was difficult to define, however, by analyzing the imaginary part of the Jost function, $\Im J(\omega)$, we identified a specific energy, $\omega_0$, at the center of the resonance, which serves as a reliable resonance indicator. By examining the RPA eigenvalue distributions, we distinguished three scenarios for the resonance: (i) a sharp peak arises when the width is small, (ii) the distribution of eigenvalues becomes scattered and difficult to define when the width is moderate, and (iii) the resonance is no longer discernible when the width is large, with many negative eigenvalues appearing. Developing a neural text generation model that can engage in a game-like scenario with another model, aiming to minimize the difference between their generated outputs, is a novel paradigm. This kind of model can be beneficial for various real-world applications such as natural language manipulation and adversarial attacks. Presently, existing methods train the adversarial model with a single objective, either using a contrastive loss function or a reinforcement learning-based approach. In contrast, we propose the SparseGAN framework, characterized by two primary features. Firstly, it employs a contrastive loss function. Secondly, it incorporates a sparse sampling technique to generate more challenging input samples. Experimentally, we demonstrated that the proposed SparseGAN model excels in both standard text generation evaluation and a game-like evaluation. Furthermore, compared to baseline models, SparseGAN effectively prevents adversarial attacks and significantly outperforms them in natural language manipulation. By incorporating a diverse set of input samples, we also explored the generalization of SparseGAN to various sampling strategies. Ultimately, our framework and experimentally-derived guidelines are both valuable for practitioners seeking to deploy the SparseGAN model in real-world settings. A hypothetical scenario involving the transport of microbial life forms within interstellar comets that have been affected by the sun is considered here. The potential effects on both comet and microorganisms as they approach the inner regions of the solar system are examined, along with the various astrophysical contexts in which this encounter might happen, such as the vicinity of giant planets or within their capture zones. A focus is placed on the possible signs of an encounter with a life-bearing comet, including the launch of high-speed comets that could carry life, the presence of certain comet sizes, and the distinct patterns of captured solar system objects. If such indicators are looked for across suitable datasets that include the orbits of long-period comets, capture zones of giant planets like Jupiter or Saturn, or the composition of microorganisms in extreme environments, then it may be possible to detect evidence of interstellar panspermia. A calculation is provided to estimate the likelihood of finding life on one of these comets or in these extreme environments, assuming that the distribution of life-bearing comets is random and taking into account the number of relevant comets or microorganisms that need to carry life in order to produce a detectable signal. Our 'Testing as Testing Includes Failing' premise suggests that testing aims to discover and correct both flaws in programs and inadequate test cases. To achieve this, we introduce a new type of test case called a 'counter-example', which can be created using our geometric method. By taking a program's geometric representation and removing the corresponding points, counter-examples can be generated through a series of natural operations that preserve correctness. To facilitate counter-example reduction, we developed a specific set of hyperplane reductions, demonstrating that any program flaw is connected to a minimal point (or points) and can be reached via these reductions. This connection enables the determination of necessary test data by identifying the points surrounding a program, as well as providing strategies for adequate test case generation. To illustrate this approach, we use an example from the safety critical industry. To facilitate counter-example reduction, we developed the 'CETool' system, a Python implementation of our method that includes the 'cereduce' tool, capable of efficiently handling large-scale reductions with complex points and surfaces. This tool has been successfully used in industry settings, notably in the testing of an Airbus flight control system. To further contribute, we outline a general protocol for program testing that we believe represents a breakthrough in the testing field. This protocol, in line with our testing premise, emphasizes the creation of adequate test cases through a process that is closely tied to program testing itself. This connection allows for the direct use of test case creation as evidence in itself, eliminating the need for additional, often subjective, assessments. This protocol has been successfully applied in a real-world setting, notably in the testing of an Ericsson telephony system. Aging networks, such as transportation systems, electricity grids, and the internet, are prone to malfunctions and attacks from unidentified sources, and due to a lack of central control, their fundamental management properties remain unclear. This work explores the limits of a specific kind of network task, called network scale estimation, which assesses a network's total in a global setting, in the presence of small numbers of attacking nodes. It is shown that, in networks with a small world property, of a specific kind, collaborative nodes can accurately calculate the network's size even with a large number of attacking nodes. However, if the network's switching probability falls below a certain threshold, recruiting new nodes does not aid in this calculation, indicating that a reduction in the network's size does not necessarily lead to a reduction in the calculation difficulty. This finding is further supported by Monte Carlo simulations. This work also highlights the significance of controlling the parameter that defines the small world property and the impact of attacks on the network's structure by providing an approximate expression that reflects the minimum required cooperation to calculate the network's size with precision. This expression is derived by developing a new, simplified model called the configuration model mixed with degree disloyalty, which offers insights into the changes in the network's average degree and the proportion of attacking nodes, and thus, in turn, affects the ease of this calculation. This model can be used to study other network tasks in a similar manner. This research was conducted without any external funding. In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our novel approach, called Complex Time-Kinematic Curvature, transforms these constraints into a hyperbolic type of curvature equation. By assuming the metric variables have a specific complex conformal structure, this approach can be applied to the Hamiltonian constraint, and combining it with the momentum constraint results in a complex Einstein's conformal field equation. Ultimately, this leads to a solution for the metric variables through a series of intermediate complex variables. We have successfully tested CTK by applying it to black hole collisions and compact binary mergers, and our method is highly efficient and accurate, outperforming existing techniques by several orders of magnitude. This approach has significant potential benefits for the soltion of the Hamiltonian constraint in numerical relativity, and can be an important tool for producing accurate simulations of complex gravitational systems. Our code, named CTK, is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/CTKproject/CTK. This paper focuses on the on-shell Higgs sector within the MSSM with complex parameters, using a SUSY-QCD analogue to guide the approach. By applying the 'tree-level' approximation, we incorporate the effects of SUSY breaking into the MSSM Higgs mass terms. This method allows us to calculate Higgs masses at the tree level, which can be compared with experimental data, thus constraining the complex parameters of the MSSM. By matching the on-shell Higgs mass matrix to that obtained from the 'tree-level' approximation, we can calculate the on-shell mass eigenvalues and CKKB angles for the neutral and charged Higgs bosons. The contextual linear bandit model has numerous applications in personalization across various contexts, and it has received significant interest in recent years. A key setting in this context is a distributed version, where an agent makes decisions in non-stationary contextual linear bandits in multiple contexts, without knowing the parameters, and then shares the learned context with the decision-maker, without needing to know the parameters as well. In this paper, we concentrate on finding an approximate optimal policy for the agent in a variety of general scenarios, with non-communicative communication constraints between the agent and the decision-maker, with contexts shared freely. We propose an algorithm called "distributed Bayesian linear bandits" and show that it yields a cumulative regret of at least $ \tilde{O}(B^{2/3} \sqrt{C T})$ in a variety of scenarios, with contexts $B$, time steps $T$, and a specific matrix dimension $C$. This is the first algorithm of its kind with a proven bound on the cumulative regret in a variety of scenarios. We also show that a previously proposed algorithm called "distributed Bayesian linear bandits with phase changes" yields a cumulative regret of at least $\tilde{O}( \sqrt{B T} + \sqrt{C T})$ in a different scenario, with contexts $B$, time steps $T$, and a specific matrix dimension $C$. The novel technique we developed for this paper involves a combination of the "explore then commit" strategy with the UCB algorithm, with a focus on finding a near-optimal policy in a variety of general scenarios. The results we obtained can be interpreted as a positive answer to the challenge posed in "Learning in contextual linear bandits without sharing the context" for the "explore then commit" strategy with the UCB algorithm. The proposed algorithm we developed for this paper is also applicable in a variety of scenarios with changes in the parameters, with non-stationary contextual linear bandits, with contexts shared freely, and it yields a cumulative regret of at least $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{C T})$ in a different scenario, with time steps $T$ and a specific matrix dimension $C$. Our study re-examines the impact of event shape variables, specifically the number of participants, the number of collisions, and the centrality, on the elliptic flow coefficient, $v_2$, in high-energy heavy-ion collisions. We utilize the HYDRO+ model to determine if a correlation exists between the average transverse momentum, $\langle p_T \rangle$, and $v_2$, and if it depends on the particle species. Our results show that this connection holds independently of the event shape, as does its species dependence. We also find that the influence of the event shape on $v_2$ is solely a result of its effect on $\langle p_T \rangle$. Consequently, our research indicates that $v_2$ can be accurately determined by analyzing inclusive $\langle p_T \rangle$ rather than requiring information about the event shape. This approach is validated through comparisons with experimental data obtained from the LHC. Our findings imply that the initial state conditions can be inferred without directly knowing the event shape, providing valuable insights into the early stages of heavy-ion collisions. Our research was originally published in Physical Review C.

This work uncovers novel insights into the performance of basic power control methods, specifically binary and optimal power control, in an interference network with an extreme signal-to-interference ratio imbalance. We demonstrate that for binary power control, there are specific scenarios where this control method can provide a significantly large (proportional to the square root of $K$) performance improvement over optimal power control, with one of these scenarios allowing for a precise estimation of this performance difference as $\sqrt{K}$. On the other hand, we also discovered an upper and a lower bound that the difference in performance can take, both being proportional to $\sqrt{K}$. Consequently, binary power control can offer a benefit of at least $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ but no more than $\Theta(\sqrt{n})$ in exchange for the increased energy consumption. This finding can be especially valuable for many real-world scenarios, such as cellular networks, where there are many users. It's worth noting that one of the key tools used in this research was a previously unknown upper bound for the sum of the square of an array's largest element. This upper bound, in turn, was derived from a novel entropy inequality, specifically for the mentioned $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ scenario. This research was originally published in the IEEE Information Theory and Applications Workshop proceedings in 2019 under the name "The Extremal GDoF Benefit of Optimal versus Binary Power Control in $K$ User Interference Networks Is $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$". It was later featured in the IEEE Transactions on Information Theory journal in 2023. It has the DOI https://doi.org/10.1109/TIT.2023.9737361 and ARXIV 2301.06245. It was also presented at the 2020 IEEE Information Theory and Applications Workshop, 2019 Allerton Conference on Communication, Control and Computing, and 2020 Annual Allerton Conference on Communication, Control and Computing. A new modeling approach is proposed to simulate multiple interacting particles with different sizes and surface properties by leveraging collision physics. In this method, larger particles are simulated using a direct numerical integration based on Navier-Stokes equations, while smaller particles are modeled using a Lagrangian approach. The model includes interactions such as hydrodynamic interactions with larger particles, inter-particle collisions with forces resulting from particle interactions, and external forces such as gravity and wall interactions. A key innovation is the incorporation of physical collision time, derived from the relative velocities and sizes of colliding particles, which allows for realistic simulation of particle interactions. A simplified multiple-time-step integration scheme is then developed to efficiently perform the simulations, tailoring time steps for both small and large particles to accurately capture both short-range collisions and long-range hydrodynamic interactions. The model's effectiveness is demonstrated through simulations of a single small particle interacting with a larger particle, both in confined environments and in the presence of a wall, as well as the simulation of sedimentation of small particles in a suspension surrounding a large particle. The results show that even a single-time-step simulation can yield collision dynamics similar to the multiple-time-step method, yet the multiple-time-step approach more accurately captures the details of both short-range collisions and long-range interactions, even in the presence of a wall. The proposed model also highlights the significance of collision time in the range of a millisecond, as well as the influence of the time steps used in simulations, providing a framework for the simulation of multiple interacting particles that can be applied to a broad range of scenarios, from the sedimentation of particles to the flow of complex fluids in microchannels. This article presents a novel proof for a notable conjecture made by Beck, LeVeque, and Guy, which stated that for all natural numbers n, there exist whole number solutions for A, B, and C in the equation $A^2+A*B+B^2= C^7*7^n$. Our argumentation leverages a specific factorization of quadratic polynomials and number theory principles, including the use of a particular property of 7 and its prime factorization. We also introduce a related problem that can be solved using our proof method. Our original proof does not incorporate any mathematical induction. In fact, we show that for the specific value of n=1, the solutions are bounded, which hinders any potential generalization of our proof using induction. In addition to addressing the aforementioned conjecture, our paper also delves into the exploration of a related problem, specifically finding the smallest natural number k such that for all natural numbers n, there exist whole number solutions for A, B in the equation $A^2+A*B+B^2= (7*7^k)^n$. We also provide an initial bound for this number k. Our proof method for both problems relies on the use of a specific property of 7 and its prime factorization, which we believe is a crucial characteristic that could be instrumental in extending our results to other prime numbers. As a side note, we found it interesting to examine the solutions for the equation $A^2+A*B+B^2= C^7*7^n$ when the value of n is equal to 3, which may provide another example for the type of patterns we mentioned earlier. We intend for this observation to serve as a potential starting point for further research. Our paper also includes a list of open problems. We believe that these problems could be addressed using our proof method, which we have made accessible for further extension and modification. Our paper provides a starting point for these problems and offers some preliminary results that could be useful for the further development of their solutions. We have made our proof method a subject of discussion in the appendix, which includes a list of open problems that we have identified as significant conjectures that could be verified, or we could determine that they are false, based on a single example. We have also included some preliminary results for these problems in the appendix. Our paper has been organized into the following sections: introduction, whole number solutions for $a^2+ab+b^2=7^n$, a related problem, the property of 7

A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the appearance of rough and soft terrain, which can hinder the performance of robots by causing them to lose balance and stability. To address this challenge, we are developing a simulated environment filled with varied terrain, as well as control systems for robots. In this research, we focused on a monopod model to study the fundamental aspects of stability and balance. We used a hybrid simulation approach that combines physical and mathematical modeling and it provided a high-fidelity simulation of the real world. However, it also made the simulation more challenging due to the time-consuming process of solving the differential algebraic equations. We enhanced the simulation model by introducing a simplified physical model that still captured the essential dynamics of the monopod. Furthermore, we developed an advanced control system based on the "fun-to-learn" framework, which helped the robot learn safe trajectories through complex environments. In the simulations, the monopod successfully navigated various obstacles and uneven terrain while preserving its stability. To accommodate softer terrain, we modified the simulation model by introducing a nonlinear contact model, which enabled the robot to determine safe learning intervals and avoid uncomfortable movements, leading to a more efficient learning process. The results showed that the monopod was capable of discovering multiple stable control policies that allowed it to move freely on soft terrain by simply altering its learning environment, which in turn allowed it to move on more difficult terrain once it had sufficient experience. The developed model and simulation were validated by comparing the measured and simulated values of the contact forces, which showed that the simulation accurately replicated the real-world scenario. The nature of dense matter within the cores of compact stars remains unclear, which in turn hinders our understanding of specific types of dense matter, including strange quark matter. A class of dense matter models, capable of supporting neutron star mass beyond 2 solar masses, has been theoretically proposed as a reference for dense matter studies. However, such models are only distinguishable from neutron star matter through the measurement of specific properties, particularly the sound speed, as a function of density. 

A study is presented here which maps the relationship between the sound speed and density in dense matter, assuming it behaves according to a Baym-Pethick-Sutherland equation of state, and subsequently determines the corresponding density dependence of the sound speed for 2 types of dense matter: neutron star matter and strange quark matter. It is shown that while the sound speed in strange quark matter is self-consistently greater than in neutron star matter above certain densities, the accuracy of this distinction depends on the precision of the sound speed measurements. 
For the sound speed to be an accurate differentiator between these 2 types of matter, it must be measured with a precision of at least 3% for densities above 3 times the saturation density of nuclear matter. This finding is significant because even if future observations do reveal a precise density dependence of the sound speed, it would necessitate a revision of the existing understanding of neutron star matter behavior, with far-reaching implications for the underlying physics governing it. 
On the other hand, if the density dependence of the sound speed is found to be inaccurate, it would suggest that compact stars with masses just above 2 solar masses could be made of strange quark matter, a possibility that has important consequences for the low to medium density behavior of quark matter, and would also provide valuable insights into the physics governing dense matter, by highlighting the role of fluctuations in nucleon and diquark densities. 
This would be particularly evident in the neutrino cooled inner crust of neutron stars, where the onset of quark matter density occurs, and could have a direct impact on the predicted dimensions of the inner crust, and would also provide a more nuanced explanation for the measured sound speed in the inner crust, and would further imply that the observed behavior in the inner crust could serve as a probe of the underlying physics governing dense matter, rather than just providing a differentiator between neutron star and quark matter.

A phenomenon called vertical shear instability (VSI) is observed in protoplanetary disk systems, and the cause behind it remains unknown. Observations suggest that the outer regions of these disks are less unstable than the mid regions, and could be stable for all known parameters. Researchers previously found that the VSI might be triggered by the movement of dust particles relative to gas, but more recent findings show that the VSI could also be influenced by the change in dust particle size. A recent study aims to investigate how changes in dust particle size affect the VSI, particularly in the outer regions of the disks. Using a simplified model and a local approach in the linear regime, scientists found that even if the conditions are favorable for VSI, the instability might eventually die out as the disks evolve and the rotation speed in the outer regions slows down, due to an increase in the radial width of the disk. Furthermore, a comparison of their results with observations shows that the timescales for dust growth and the evolution of the disks are too long to be distinguishable, but the former could result in the VSI becoming unstable in the mid regions of the disks, while the latter might lead to the VSI becoming unstable in the inner regions, and even affect the development of VSI in the outer regions by making the disks more or less unstable, depending on their growth or shrinkage. On the other hand, a non-linear analysis of the VSI reveals that the VSI might eventually give way to a different type of instability called the dipolar instabilities, and could significantly influence the development of the inner regions of the disks by causing the formation of density waves and affecting the development of the VSI in the outer regions, and even leading to the formation of planets if it results in the formation of a baroclinic instability in the inner regions. Consequently, a thorough, non-linear analysis of the VSI is necessary to gain a better understanding of the effects it has on the formation of planets in protoplanetary disk systems. This research focuses on harmonic functions within the context of a particular type of manifold where the Ricci curvature decreases over time and the scalar curvature remains constant. We have derived a key theorem demonstrating that bounded harmonic functions are constant in this specific type of manifold, without relying on an established growth estimate. Consequently, this result implies that the set of all harmonic functions that grow in a compact manner is finite-dimensional. We have also demonstrated that this scenario cannot occur in a particular type of manifold defined by a specific equation and has a compact structure. Ultimately, this leads to the conclusion that the latter type of manifold is compact. This, in turn, paves the way for an alternate proof of a previously established fact. Additionally, this result has a significant implications for another type of manifold where the curvature satisfies certain growth conditions, with far-reaching consequences. Lastly, this research also includes a characterization of all harmonic functions within the context of another type of manifold, with further implications discussed in the concluding section. Recent advancements in outsourcing training and machine learning as a service have created innovative threats such as hidden functionalities that are embedded in artificial neural networks. In typical scenarios, a malicious trainer can conceal their ulterior motives by manipulating only a portion of the input, taking advantage of how information is processed in networks. However, in this research, we are concentrating on developing techniques that go beyond this limitation and allow a malicious trainer to influence the network's behavior based on the entire input, even after it has been processed and the input has been pooled globally. Our research specifically targets networks that incorporate a global mean pooling layer and determines the conditions under which such networks can be manipulated, as well as a learning framework that can be used to train these networks, on condition that the training data is compromised. Furthermore, we demonstrate the applicability of our framework in real-world scenarios through tests on hidden functionalities in networks used for image classification and language processing. Our results show that networks with a global mean pooling layer can be effectively manipulated, and even tiny amounts of compromised data can lead to significant threats to safety in networks used for language processing. Our research on hidden functionalities in networks used for image classification allows us to surpass the previous benchmark for accuracy by developing a new attack called the overparameterized attack, which requires only a tiny amount of compromised data. Our research has important implications for how networks with a global mean pooling layer can be trusted in real-world applications. Individuals within the criminal justice system are experiencing mental health crises at an alarming rate, with estimates suggesting that 2 out of every 3 prisoners are afflicted by some form of mental disorder.  This study seeks to investigate a novel aspect of mental health treatment within the justice system - the impact of court-ordered mental health treatment for individuals convicted of crimes.  To achieve this, researchers analyzed data from the North Carolina prison system from 2001 to 2015, taking into account various factors such as prison conditions, mental health treatment, as well as inmate characteristics.  Taking a difference-in-differences approach and comparing both prisoners serving sentences and those on probation, the study found that court-ordered mental health treatment reduces reincarceration rates by 5.5% to 12% and lowers the likelihood of violent reincarceration by 9% to 20%.  The study also discovered that the therapeutic effect of treatment is more pronounced among prisoners with severe mental disorders, individuals who have prior convictions, and those serving longer sentences.  Estimating the therapeutic impact of treatment as a function of treatment duration, the study found that even brief treatment can significantly reduce reincarceration rates.  Finally, the findings suggest that funding for mental health treatment in North Carolina during this period was inefficiently allocated, with a greater return on investment derived from treating prisoners serving sentences than those on probation.  The study's results hold valuable implications for justice and mental health policymakers, highlighting the potential of court-ordered treatment to reduce recidivism rates and suggesting that targeted, long-term treatment programs could yield the best results.  The study's methodology and findings also offer a framework for evaluating the effectiveness of justice system interventions aimed at addressing mental health disorders. To address this issue, a new regularization technique called Consistency by Switching has been developed, which focuses on making the model's predictions consistent when switching between two differently trained models. This technique can be an alternative to more complex GAN-based methods, offering a more straightforward solution to semi-supervised image segmentation tasks. Experiments using a widely used dataset demonstrated the efficacy of this technique, as it outperformed a baseline model and alternative methods in many cases. The development of Consistency by Switching provides a starting point for future research into the regularization of medical image segmentation tasks. This operator acts on holomorphic functions defined on $X$. Under the assumption that $X$ is compact, this operator is surjective. In this paper, we prove that it is also surjective when $X$ is not compact, provided that the dimension of $X$ is one and the variety has no compact components. Recent advances in deep learning, particularly transfer learning, have revolutionized speech recognition systems. It has become possible to achieve high accuracy without constructing vast amounts of labeled training data. In our research, we explored two speech recognition applications where transfer learning excels: cross institutional evaluation and multilingual models. Our main contribution involves two novel strategies to enhance speech recognition performance: a proposed method to seamlessly integrate time dynamics and another utilizing a coarse-to-fine decoding process. Our findings show that these innovations yield a 8.5% improvement in cross institutional evaluation and a 5.2% increase in multilingual models. By combining our proposed methods with other leading techniques, our research achieves state-of-the-art results in cross institutional evaluation and multilingual models, surpassing the records set in "Translating Transferable Knowledge for Cross Institutional ASR" and "Multilingual End-to-End Multi-speaker Speech Recognition" by 2.3% and 3.2% respectively. Furthermore, our work on time dynamics' representation enables a new record in the "SuperHuman" benchmark, surpassing "DeepTracK" by 3.6%. Our research on the coarse-to-fine process yields results comparable to the baseline, but our findings indicate that this method could be effective for other difficult decoding challenges.
