We employ a 1+1+2 covariant semi-tetrad method to describe a relativistic, anisotropic, and dissipative stellar object within Einstein's general relativity. By utilizing a specific anisotropic dual-fluid model as an example, we derive general equations describing the relation between anisotropic stress-energy tensors and derive explicit expressions for the relativistic surface area, temperature distribution, and barotropic pressure profiles. Additionally, we calculate the entropy density, bulk viscosity, and surface gravity in the context of this model. By comparing our derived expressions with existing limits, we demonstrate how the anisotropic stress-energy relation can transform from general to specific forms, thus providing a framework for modeling various complex phenomena within the anisotropic dual-fluid model. This approach enables a unified and versatile formulation, allowing for the computation of multiple physical quantities in the context of this model. This anisotropic dual-fluid framework has implications for the study of relativistic rotating stars, electromagnetic wave propagation within dense nuclear matter, and the behavior of matter at high densities in general relativity. This approach may also serve as a foundation for investigating other complex phenomena, such as magneto-rotational instability and neutrino-cooled accretion disks. Most current sequence-to-sequence based Grammatical Error Correction methods focus primarily on generating more diverse and high-quality training data. However, these approaches overlook the challenge of adapting to new domains with limited annotated data. This paper addresses this domain adaptation challenge by integrating GEC tasks into a meta-learning framework, thereby enabling the model to acquire general domain knowledge and adapt efficiently to new environments. Our proposed approach, consisting of an initial training phase with a meta-algorithm, allows for effective transfer to a new domain with just a few annotated examples. We evaluate our model on NME scores for the NEC corpus and achieve state-of-the-art results in multiple target domains, surpassing the performance of strong baselines by a significant margin. Moreover, our model demonstrates exceptional performance in domains with limited data, showing a 6.32 NME absolute improvement on average. Moreover, an in-depth analysis of feature maps using our Salient Activation Mapping technique provides valuable insights into task and domain-specific representations, facilitating targeted enhancements to our model, such as the introduction of a new evaluation task called NEC-50. This involves reducing the model's capacity to enhance performance in more challenging domains, thereby facilitating a broader exploration of the GEC domain. Using lattice QCD, a method is developed to project momentum correlations from a pion's wave function, allowing for the identification of mesons with specific quark and antiquark momenta within the pion.  This approach can distinguish between different current combinations that can project the same charge and spin properties, and provides a means to investigate the relative coefficients of different current combinations in a general two-quark system.  For the pion, results indicate that the coefficient of a specific current combination, known as "collinear currents," is substantially larger than the others, with approximately 99% of the charge density explained by these collinear currents.  This conclusion remains after accounting for errors in the calculation and variations in the method used.  This finding has implications for the interpretation of heavy meson decay lengths, suggesting that they primarily reflect the light quark's distribution rather than the heavy quark's own wave function, and highlight the importance of using charge and spin projectors instead of charge and spin-averaged currents when measuring the size of heavy meson systems.  This approach may also be applied to other light mesons, such as the kaon and heavy mesons, and can be a valuable tool for extracting information about the wave functions of hadrons from lattice QCD calculations.  This research was conducted using data from the Highly Improved Staggered Quarks ensemble.  A discussion of the method used to project momentum correlations is presented in [1], and this approach can be a starting point for more complex analyses, such as those described in [2, 3].  A more detailed explanation of the results and their implications is available in [4]. We developed a novel approach to register MV images, utilizing a Convolutional Neural Network, in both 2D and 3D. Traditional alignment techniques are largely based on optimization methods that require precise initialization, yet often struggle with converging to a correct solution, particularly when comparing Dose Megavoltage (MV) images and Kiloelectronvolt (kV) images. Our training data consisted of unaligned MV image pairs, which we transformed into 3D volumes, aligning them with kV images obtained through CT scans. We used these pairs to train a U-Net, which produced 3D aligned volumes, subsequently using these results to develop a simple evaluation metric. By applying this network in a sliding window fashion, we were able to generate a 3D registration of a single MV image in relation to a kV image, without any initialization. Our experiments showed that this network can recover meaningful information when converging to a local optimum, resulting in a 3D registration comparable to gold standard BIRDMEND registrations, as evaluated by our metric. Moreover, this network can be used to generate 3D volumes from limited-angle kV images, enabling the creation of synthetic kV images for purposes such as dose estimation on the torso. When comparing 2D and 3D alignments, we found that both yielded comparable results, with the choice of dimensionality primarily influencing the amount of memory utilized. Finally, our code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghassan72/MV-image-registration.

In our research, we compared and contrast single-particle steering with the EPR paradox, single-particle entanglement, and Bell nonlocality, examining how these phenomena behave under different scenarios, including the influence of decoherence, threshold values for necessary conditions, and the need for specific types of measurements. We also recognized a genuine non-reality-based effect - particle steering - by exploring the relationship between reality constraints and the success of a particular measurement task, which can be achieved without resorting to the use of entanglement. A proposed precoder codebook and feedback encoding approach leverages Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to reduce information exchange between transmitter and receiver. Initially, a GMM is trained to capture channel distribution, then codebooks are created based on GMM components, with corresponding indices transmitted instead of precoder values. As a result, the amount of feedback is substantially decreased, with an average of 2.32 bits per symbol in a 4x4 system, compared to 16. This concise feedback enables accurate reconstruction of efficient precoders, with performance loss less than 2% compared to optimal precoders. Evaluation across various FDD scenarios confirms the system's effectiveness. Furthermore, an analytical expression is derived for the codeword index distribution, leading to an efficient batch feedback encoding method. This approach's limitations are also examined, with suggestions for improved performance. Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One key factor limiting the widespread use of text games in testing agent capabilities is their slow simulation speed.
To address this constraint, a high-performance framework called TextWorldExpress is presented, which achieves a remarkable speed of one million actions per second on average.
By leveraging GPU acceleration and a novel asynchronous pipeline, TextWorldExpress significantly boosts simulation efficiency without sacrificing crucial safety and fairness properties.
As a result, the platform can efficiently support challenging text games with numerous participants, as seen in the recent TextWorld Marathon competition, by accelerating simulations of up to 65 times on a single GPU.
TextWorldExpress is an open-source tool that is available for use and further development.

Deep learning models such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) have achieved superior performance in various sequence analysis tasks. However, their extensive size prevents them from being utilized on most FPGA-based hardware for real-time applications. This research focuses on creating an energy-efficient LSTM network capable of real-time video identification. The novel LSTM model, named ELSTM, features a compact design with approximately one-tenth the parameters of a standard LSTM. To further enhance efficiency, a Hierarchical Tucker Tensor Decomposition (HTTD) algorithm is developed to reduce the network's size to a millionth of its original size while maintaining performance, and a custom hardware platform is designed to execute the compressed network. The results demonstrate that the energy-efficient ELSTM network, implemented on a hardware platform consisting of 1024 tiny LUT-based processing elements, can process 108 frames per second on a single FPGA, surpassing similar previous works. The novel HTTD algorithm developed in this research can also be applied to other deep learning models. A current theory suggests that Venus' surface temperature and atmospheric composition were significantly different in the past, approximately mimicking those of Earth. This hypothesis is based on geological evidence revealing Venus' surface age is around 500 million years, roughly half the planet's estimated 4.5 billion years. To investigate this historical atmosphere, we simulated the atmosphere's evolution over time, accounting for various processes such as greenhouse effect, atmospheric escape, tectonic activity, and solar energy. By adjusting key factors, we aimed to identify critical events that shaped the atmosphere's current state. One key finding suggests that a runaway greenhouse phase lasted around 200 million years, ultimately leading to the present state of the atmosphere. Another important discovery is that the timescale for atmospheric escape's effect on hydrogen to become noticeable was found to be around 1-10 million years, significantly shorter than previously estimated. Furthermore, we found that the current rate of hydrogen escape is sufficient to strip the planet of its remaining water in less than 10 million years, implying the planet must have experienced a significant water loss event in the past. This study introduces a novel occurrence where extremely powerful linearly polarized laser pulses encounter a specific target and, as a result, switch to circular polarization while significantly increasing their overall intensity. We address the case of rank metric codes under the assumption that a code with parameters $[n,k,r]$ has an extremely large distance $r$, making it nearly maximally distant. This condition allows us to treat these codes as codes with parameters $[n,k]$ and consider their decoding in the presence of symmetric rank errors. Our main achievement is the development of an efficient decoding algorithm for these codes, even those with list-decoding or unique word properties, by utilizing the Euclidean distance as a ranking measure. This algorithm is effective in identifying the smallest rank error and can be used as a precursor to other decoding algorithms, such as the algorithm developed by Kotter and Krasicki, or the Bard-Gabidulin decoding for some cases, all of which have a significant drawback of being notoriously hard to implement due to their high computational complexity. We also explore the distribution of the Euclidean distances between valid codewords and highlight the asymptotic behavior of this distribution as the distance $r$ approaches its maximum value, thereby shedding new light on the structure of rank metric codes. Finally, we discuss the implications of our results for the code's minimum distance, its block structure, and a specific class of codes, along with several open problems. Ultimately, our research was motivated by the desire to explore the distribution of the Euclidean distances between valid codewords, which in turn arose from the study of decoding strategies, specifically the need to compare two decoding algorithms with different ranking measures. We believe that the code's minimum distance and block structure, as well as the asymptotic behavior of the Euclidean distance distribution, all constitute interesting research topics that can be studied independently of the decoding strategies. On the other hand, the asymptotic analysis of the Euclidean distance distribution allows us to establish a bound on the code's minimum distance, which in turn allows us to classify codes with unique words as well as determine the effectiveness of one decoding algorithm compared to another. We also discuss the similarity between rank metric codes and codes with unique words and highlight the differences between the two, which we believe can be further explored in the future. We believe that our research resonates with the work of Kotter and Krasicki as well as the research on list decoding, which we discuss in the paper. We hope that our results, specifically the asymptotic analysis of the Euclidean distance distribution, will be beneficial to future research. We obtained high-cadence photometric and spectroscopic data for SN~2020jfo in various wavelengths starting around day 3 up to day 540 from its explosion. SN~2020jfo, classified as a hydrogen-rich Type II supernova with a short plateau duration, is remarkable for having one of the briefest plateau phases ever recorded. By comparing it with two other supernovae that also have extended hydrogen absorption lines, SN~2020jfo falls into the transitional phase between the classical and shallow II supernovae. It also exhibits a stronger nebula phase than the other two supernovae, both photometrically and spectroscopically. Furthermore, we estimate its host galaxy's stellar mass and star formation rate as 10 to the power of 9 and 0.5 to 1.0 solar masses per year, respectively. SN~2020jfo's progenitor star is estimated to have 10 to the power of 5.5 solar masses with a margin of error and a radius of 10 to the power of 11 to the power of 5.5 solar radii with a similar margin, and it exploded with a massive explosion energy of 10 to the power of 49 ergs. Finally, we discuss SN~2020jfo's intriguing characteristics and propose that its progenitor was likely a massive supergiant within a tight binary system.

The development of wide-field X-ray monitoring is a growing area of interest, with applications in astrophysical time-domain studies and nuclear non-proliferation efforts. To achieve the desired all-sky coverage, a lobster-eye (LE) X-ray optics arrangement is being explored, with the potential to greatly reduce the number of detectors required. We investigate a variant of LE optics called the "multiplexed lobster-eye" design, in which multiple LE arrays are arranged in a 2D grid, with the aim of determining a suitable layout that minimizes the number of detectors while maintaining a high sky coverage. We evaluate the performance of a proposed 16x16 LE array configuration, with a 1.5 degree field of view, and find it could cover over 90% of the sky with 10,000 detectors, compared to 30,000 required for a non-multiplexed LE array of the same field of view. We also analyze the optical response of the multiplexed arrangement and validate our results using Monte Carlo simulations of the light transport within the optics. With its complex optical performance and the potential for 3D fabrication, the multiplexed LE design presents a promising and versatile option for wide-field X-ray monitoring. We propose a prototype to demonstrate this concept, with a compact 4x4 configuration that could be easily scaled up to larger formats. We discuss the potential applications and future developments of this design, including its compatibility with modern CMOS detectors and folding mirror arrangements that could further increase the sky coverage. We also outline a path for the Monte Carlo simulations used in our study to be integrated with other design tools, such as ray-tracing codes, to accelerate the development of this and similar optics. We estimate that a 64x64 multiplexed LE arrangement could detect a 10^-8 ph/s signal with a 10^3 s exposure, and we discuss the prospects for demonstrating this performance with a prototype using the National Spherical Aberration Corrector (NAC) X-ray beamline. With its unique optical performance, the multiplexed LE design presents a promising and versatile option for wide-field X-ray monitoring, and we believe it has the potential to contribute to a variety of scientific and security-related time-domain studies. We propose a research agenda for this design, with the aim of advancing the field of X-ray optics and the performance of this particular arrangement, with the ultimate goal of developing a 64x64 multiplexed LE arrangement capable of detecting a 10^-8 ph/s

Document extraction models have numerous practical uses, given the vast amount of printed content requiring digital conversion. Nonetheless, labeling documents is labor-intensive and expensive due to the need for precise annotations. Current model training relies on lengthy and costly processes involving extensive data sets, with estimates suggesting the cost of 100,000 labeled documents being around $750,000. This study presents a cost-efficient approach to document extraction, leveraging unannotated documents to a significant extent. It achieves this by adapting a contrastive unsupervised learning technique, which leverages documents with inadequate annotations, as well as a self-training method that refines these annotations without human intervention. The resulting model excels at accurately annotating new documents with a mere 1,000 labeled documents, achieving an F1 score of 0.83 and a SPRec score of 0.79 in our evaluation. When put to use on real-world tasks, it extracts relevant information from unannotated documents with a high degree of precision, as evidenced by our case study involving Congressional reports. The developed approach provides a significant reduction in labeling costs, with estimates suggesting $187,500 for 100,000 labeled documents. The code for this project is available online at GitHub at this link: https://github.com/nyukto/unsup-document-extraction. However, for binary neutron star mergers below a certain Chirp Mass threshold, the signal analysis faces difficulties in identifying components through post-merger oscillations and binary coalescence. A key challenge lies in distinguishing between binary neutron star and neutron star-black hole mergers of similar chirp masses, given the limited information available from gravitational waves. An in-depth examination of daily interactions in a significant number of urban areas across the world has provided insights into how people's social behaviors have changed since the COVID-19 pandemic began. By analyzing survey data from over 100 cities, this research reveals that urban residents' average number of daily interactions decreased by a third on average, with variations ranging from a tenth to a half, depending on the city. Not only did the overall decline in interactions notable, but there were also significant differences in how much they decreased in different cities. For instance, cities like Auckland, where people reduced their interactions by more than a half, were on one end of the spectrum, while cities like Madrid, where the decrease was less than a tenth, were on the other. Furthermore, this study found that cities with smaller decreases in interactions tended to have more diverse income levels, whereas cities with larger decreases in interactions had less income diversity. In fact, the data showed that the income diversity in these cities was a third to a half less than it would have been normally. Additionally, this research discovered that the income diversity in cities with more even distributions of daily interactions was also even more diverse, as they had a quarter to a third more income diversity than average, whereas cities with more uneven distributions had a quarter to a half less income diversity than average. Interestingly, the data revealed that the decline in interactions and income diversity varied little across different age groups, although younger adults were slightly more likely to reduce their interactions. On the other hand, the changes differed more significantly across different education levels, with people who had a higher education reducing their interactions more than those with lower levels of education, as well as those living in urban versus rural areas, where the decline in interactions was greater in urban areas, and finally, the changes also differed more significantly across different income levels, with people in higher income brackets reducing their interactions more than those in lower income brackets. Notably, the data showed that the decline in interactions was more significant in cities where people reduced their interactions more had lower growth rates in income diversity, as well as in face-to-face interactions in public spaces, compared to cities where people reduced their interactions less, as well as in crowds and in private spaces, although the relationship between these variables changed over time. The formation of massive stars is crucial for understanding the chemical composition and evolution of the universe, yet the process of their formation remains poorly understood. It is widely accepted that massive protostars form from a massive core, but the specifics of their formation, including the role of accretion, external influences such as gravity from nearby stars or gas, and the effect of their surroundings on their development, are not well known. This paper explores the formation of massive stars by modeling a massive core with a low to medium density environment, and finds that the accretion of dense material during the formation of massive stars often occurs in rapid, intense episodes that can result in the merger of smaller protostars. It further suggests that the common observation of massive stars on the main sequence in binary or multiple star systems may be the result of such mergers, and that these mergers can also lead to the rapid formation of low-mass stars. We develop a novel iterative method to solve the $\ell_1$-norm principal component analysis problem, a key issue in high-dimensional data analysis. We also establish a theoretical relationship between the optimal solution and a single iteration of our method. Building upon this relationship, we demonstrate that our algorithm is guaranteed to produce a linearly convergent sequence whose members differ from the optimal solution by a factor inversely proportional to the square of the number of iterations. For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings, having an effective representation of their environment is crucial. In this context, we are focusing on navigation through unknown environments without prior knowledge. Current methods often use direct mappings between observations and actions, represented by reinforcement learning and neural networks, which can lead to issues such as getting stuck in local minima and difficulty in generalizing to new situations. In contrast, we propose a novel representation called HiTMap (Hierarchical Topological Map), a graph-based model that combines a coarse grid map for global navigation with node-based sub-grids for more in-depth exploration, without pre-defining the structure. Through simulation tests, we found HiTMap to outperform the current state-of-the-art method in most cases, also successfully generalizing to new environments. Furthermore, we have made HiTMap a publicly accessible framework on GitHub, available for download and modification. Experimental analysis on a simulated room environment revealed that HiTMap's representation retains the ability to accurately predict future states even after 1000 iterations, also demonstrating a notable increase in performance when compared to the current baseline method. Additionally, we have an upcoming plan to integrate HiTMap with a real-world robot in a laboratory setting. HiTMap's unique design offers valuable insights into the essential components of navigation in unknown environments, which can be applied to the development of more advanced models. From a broader perspective, this research falls under the category of hierarchical reinforcement learning, which can be generalized to a wide range of problems beyond navigation. In contrast to current hierarchical models that focus on complex tasks as a single unified process, we propose a different approach where individual subprocesses can be independent and distinct, also providing a novel way to combine the advantages of hierarchical and flat policies. This new method has been successfully implemented as a navigation system in the form of HiTMap. In object-based programming, memory is allocated and managed for objects within arrays, a common practice in fields like computer vision and machine learning. Despite its benefits, this approach can lead to performance issues when using GPUs, mainly due to the inherent fragmentation of object-based memory and limited parallelization potential. Our research addresses these challenges by introducing DynaSOAr, a parallel memory allocator designed specifically for object-based arrays on GPUs. By introducing a novel free memory management system and dynamic object sizing, DynaSOAr significantly reduces fragmentation and increases the efficiency of memory allocation. Additionally, DynaSOAr's compact metadata minimizes memory waste and accelerates searches for free memory and allocated objects. Our allocator is best suited for applications that employ recursive algorithms and allocate memory in a hierarchical manner. By putting our allocator through a series of modifications to existing benchmarks and algorithms, we demonstrate DynaSOAr's capabilities and potential for further improvement. By leveraging our allocator's features, developers can optimize their own object-based arrays for better performance on GPUs. Our code is available for use and modification under the permissive Apache License 2.0.

A comprehensive theoretical model has been developed to describe the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states comprising a single magnetic impurity or a cluster of impurities on a superconducting surface. This YSR state model, validated through various parameters, incorporates both magnetic interactions and retardation effects. By applying it to manganese adatoms and clusters on a niobium surface, the phase and magnitude of YSR states are determined. Contrary to isolated YSR states, the pairing of electrons is found to be disrupted in clusters with head-to-tail magnetic arrangements, even when they are close to each other, and this effect can be quite robust, remaining evident even when the magnetic interactions are weakened. This theory is relevant to recent experiments and can provide insights with new parameters. Furthermore, it highlights the unique properties of YSR states formed from a double S-type arrangement and suggests that it may serve as a model for certain phenomena in bulk materials, such as the formation of YSR bands from a chain of impurities, and the possible appearance of a double minimum or even an imaginary gap when the YSR states overlap. This finding agrees with experimental data obtained through angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy from a manganese chain on niobium and can also be applied to similar situations in other materials. The NASA $TESS$ mission's comprehensive sky survey allows the detection of small transiting planets around bright stars.  By analyzing the $TESS$ data of TOI-712, we identified three sub-Jupiter sized planets with distinct orbital periods.  Radial velocity measurements from the spectrograph ESPaDYN confirmed the planets' existence and revealed their masses.  The newly derived parameters indicate that the two longer period planets, TOI-712 b and c, have similar masses and orbital configurations, while the third planet, TOI-712 d, has a significantly shorter orbital period.  By simulating the TOI-712 system's formation, we found that TOI-712 d's close proximity to the star might have been avoidable if the system had more time to develop, and that TOI-712 may host an additional, yet undiscovered planet in the habitable zone, making it comparable to the Kepler-452 system.  The discovery of TOI-712, with its two mini-Neptune siblings and possible third planet in the habitable zone, broadens our understanding of planetary formation and suggests that some systems similar to our solar system exist.  Future observations, such as the ESPaDYN-2 instrument, which is ten times more sensitive, will be necessary to confirm the existence of the Earth-sized TOI-712 e and accurately calculate the TOI-712 system's parameters.  The data presented in this study are available online.  The discovery of TOI-712 highlights the potential for $TESS$ and future missions to detect small, rocky worlds around bright stars through the transit method and radial velocity analysis. The main issue with deploying deep learning models in real-world skin cancer diagnosis scenarios on dermatoscopic images is the presence of unusual images in testing sets. Such images frequently result in significant performance drops in model evaluations. However, the same unusual images often appear in new patient data, which can lead to the model's unreliable use in clinical settings. To address this limitation, this study first employs a deep learning-based classifier to classify samples and a strategy to detect outliers by calculating the Shannon entropy of the classifier's layer weights. Next, a custom dataset is analyzed to develop and evaluate an effective strategy for identifying unusual images and deriving a trained model to achieve superior results on commonly used datasets with minimal preprocessing. On the MNIST dataset, the model's outlier detection accuracy reaches 99.3%. On the ISIC dataset, it achieves state-of-the-art performance with AUC values of 0.967 for melanoma and 0.933 for nonmelanoma skin cancer. Finally, the model's robustness is demonstrated by achieving comparable performance with real-world data despite being trained on highly unusual image datasets. This research provides efficient, deep learning-based solutions for developing robust models and detecting unusual images, which can be applied to skin cancer diagnosis but are suitable for any image classification task. Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. We studied J/ψ decays at various energy levels, specifically for direct detection experiments like TPC and Majoron detectors, as well as on neutrino and dark matter coefficients in Effective Field Theories. We calculated the invisible decay width of J/ψ using form factors derived from its quark composition, which corresponds to 0.439 MeV. This width enables us to establish a lower bound on |m_0| based on neutrino mass, and on a coefficient in Effective Field Theories based on neutrino and dark matter interactions. We also determined the J/ψ lifetime to be less than 1.67×10^-10 seconds, and the invisible branching ratio to be (1.05±0.01)×10^-2. The ICRF test facility IShTAR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is designed to investigate how plasma interacts with radio frequency waves. A plasma source with a 0.1 meter length and 0.4 meter diameter provides plasma necessary for the experiment, and can operate in two modes: a helicon discharge, and a plasma etching mode using radio frequency waves. This study focuses on the helicon mode, a stable configuration that produces 1 ampere of plasma current using 13.56 MHz waves and 400 watts of power, and creates a plasma with 0.1 meter length, 0.04 meter diameter, and an electron temperature of 5 electron volts. To accurately model this plasma, a new version of the IShTAR plasma source code was developed, and successfully replicated the helicon mode discharge and its associated plasma when tested against actual data. This achievement enables future modeling of the helicon mode for different operating conditions, and is a crucial step towards understanding how radio frequency waves interact with the plasma.

This paper presents an image processing technique that can be applied to histopathology images containing cancer tissue. Processed images highlight the cancerous nuclei, making it easier to detect tumors. The approach uses a two-stage W-Net: in the first stage, the network reduces noise and enhances contrast, and in the second stage, it creates a binary mask for precise nucleus segmentation. When applied to images from multiple sources, it consistently produces comparable results to state-of-the-art methods while requiring significantly less computational power. The code has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghruan/wnet. The straightforward implementation enables efficient nucleus segmentation from whole images, bypassing the need for time-consuming manual annotation. The code has been optimized for CUDA and can be run on a single GPU within 24 hours to process 5000 test images. The approach has been tested on datasets containing images of prostate, lung, colon, breast, and pancreatic cancer tissue. The output of the W-Net can be downloaded from https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1B6i6z0gG6lXy6s6y6y6z0gG6lXy6s6y6z0gG. The code has been designed to accommodate large datasets, allowing the easy addition of new datasets with different types of cancer. The approach has been validated using comprehensive experiments and comparisons with state-of-the-art methods, providing valuable insights into its performance. The results show that the approach excels in noise reduction, enhances the contrast of images, and produces high-quality segmentation masks. The evaluation has been conducted using quantitative and qualitative metrics, including precision, recall, the F1-score, the Dice coefficient, the IOU, the mean squared error, the structural similarity index, and visual inspection. The results indicate that the approach produces high-quality masks for a wide range of images, achieving an F1-score of 0.85, a precision of 0.88, a recall of 0.82, a Dice coefficient of 0.83, and an IOU of 0.81 when applied to images containing lung cancer tissue, and an F1-score of 0.78, a precision of 0.82, a recall of 0.74, a Dice coefficient of 0.79, and an IOU of 0.77 when applied to images containing colon cancer tissue. This paper aims to bridge this knowledge gap by presenting an intuitive analysis of GCNN's convolution operation as a discrete matched filtering process, drawing parallels with classical radar signal processing theory. By reinterpreting this context, we uncover key insights into GCNN's properties, such as the impact of spectral convolution, ReLU activation, and max-pooling, as well as the impact of GCNN's learning to resist noise and determine optimal convolution kernels. By framing GCNN's behavior through the lens of matched filtering, we gain a more in-depth comprehension of GCNN's performance, which can be used to assess the impact of various hyperparameters on performance. This analysis also yields a simple GCNN architecture, which we test and compare to existing methods on commonly used image classification datasets. This architecture's performance is comparable to, if not better than, established methods, as demonstrated by the results presented. To address this challenge, this study introduces the Virtual Source Synthetic Aperture (VSSA) method to estimate and compensate for lateral shifts. By reconstructing images from the perspective of a virtual source located at the midpoint of the transducer array, VSSA reduces the effects of lateral shifts and elastogram formation time. Experiments using phantoms and a real-time elastography system show that the VSSA method effectively diminishes lateral shift errors, resulting in more precise stiffness estimation. When compared to the state-of-the-art Spatial Phase Correlation (SPC) method, VSSA's performance improvements become particularly evident at greater elastogram formation times. By incorporating temporal elastogram formation time into the model, VSSA also exhibits reduced stiffness estimation errors, indicating its potential to enhance the diagnostic accuracy of elastography. We introduce a novel hierarchical strategy for solving large-scale stochastic chase-evasion games on grid worlds by dividing the environment into'macro-states'. This approach combines two separate representations: a high-level model incorporating the'macro-states' and a collection of'micro-policies' for each state within those aggregates. We've developed three key techniques: a method for creating the grid's hierarchical structure, a set of'macro-actions' defined by the transition probabilities between these states, and an iterative algorithm to train the value function for the'macro-states'. By leveraging this hierarchical representation, we can significantly reduce the complexity of the model while preserving the original's scale and dynamics. When compared to other compression methods, our approach demonstrates improved performance in various chase-evasion grid worlds. The resulting model also facilitates the construction of an evader's optimal evasion strategy for a navigator in grid worlds. We then generate a "twisted" version of this system, which is able to detect the existence of a specific kind of statement that contradicts itself. The "twisted" system's own incompleteness is demonstrated by showing it is impossible to prove a crucial statement that asserts a specific type of self-referential statement exists, even though this type of statement is readily apparent within the "twisted" system itself. We also show that this self-referential statement is necessarily undecidable within the "twisted" system and cannot be proved or disproved by this system, thus providing a second, stronger form of the Gödel first incompleteness theorem. We then use this "twisted" system to create a sequence of increasingly complex systems, each with its own unique form of incompleteness, showing that it's possible to create systems of any desired level of incompleteness. We also show that these systems are all essentially equivalent to each other, yet are not able to recognize this fact, thus providing a new proof for a significant consequence of Gödel's diagonalization lemma. We end by discussing the implications of these results for certain theories about the nature of reality and knowledge, specifically the concept of "metamathematical reality" proposed by Tarski, and the distinction between abstract truth and physical reality highlighted by Carnap and Tarski. In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete signal or image based on available data. Because there can be multiple plausible solutions, researchers focus on finding the most likely one according to Bayes' theorem. This involves calculating the posterior distribution, a complex task that is typically infeasible without strong computational resources and a vast amount of training data. The interstellar scintillation of pulsar light can be utilized to uncover the characteristics of the interstellar medium. By observing the pulsar B1133+16 at high frequency, we gathered high-resolution dynamic spectra of its pulse timeseries over a decade, from 1999 to 2009. The combined data allowed us to create a 10-year long light curve for this pulsar, based on its pulse arrival time variations. The resulting curve reveals a pattern of entangled threads with different orientations in the plane of the sky, as predicted by general relativity. Additionally, we detected the effects of long-lived scintillation patterns, probably transverse modulation instability, on the pulse timeseries. By separating the effects of the pattern on the pulse timeseries, we gathered data from different lines of sight within the beam and combined them to determine the characteristics of the interstellar medium along the path to B1133+16. These characteristics include the free electron column density, magnetic field strength, turbulence strength, and the angle between the polarization of the pulse and the position vector of the observer within the beam. The results show an average electron density of 0.053 pc^-1, a turbulent strength of 0.17, a magnetic field of 4.7 microgausses and an angle of 60 degrees. Recent advancements in graph neural networks have primarily focused on Euclidean-based methods, ignoring the potential benefits of Lorentzian geometry. Our research fills this gap by introducing LGNNs, a novel framework that leverages Lorentzian geometry to enhance graph neural networks. LGNNs incorporate a unique node representation using the Lorentzian metric, allowing for efficient learning of coordinates that minimize the distance between graphs. Our analysis shows that LGNNs optimize a non-Euclidean version of the clustering objective, providing a theoretical foundation for this optimization. We further demonstrate the practical advantages of LGNNs in real-world applications by developing LGNN-based variants of popular neural network architectures, which outperform their non-Lorentzian counterparts in tasks such as node classification and clustering. Moreover, LGNNs can be trained on significantly larger graphs, leading to a new benchmark record in WebSphere. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghaleem/Lorentzian-GCN. Our findings suggest that LGNNs can be a promising alternative to conventional graph neural networks, offering improved performance in various real-world tasks.

This research focuses on a linear acoustic-structural inverse problem, where we aim to recover the details of a vibrating structure whose acoustic counterpart is observable in the sound field. Unlike direct problems, inverse problems require us to work backwards to achieve this goal. A key aspect of this study involves utilizing the relationship between the structure's and acoustic's eigenfunctions to create an algorithm for estimating the vibrating surface. A numerical example serves to illustrate the effectiveness of our method-based approach, and it shows us that even when noise is present in the data, our algorithm can successfully recover the structure's eigenvalues and modal coefficients. However, it's worth noting that our method succeeds in recovering the modal coefficients but struggles with accuracy in recovering the eigenvalues, especially when the data is noisy. This research assumes a 2D acoustic scenario with point sources, although it's feasible to adapt it for a 3D environment with distributed sources. This work also leverages the concept of a reduced order model to facilitate real-time recovery, and it's an approach that can be integrated with more complex models, such as nonlinear structures, by incorporating our algorithm into a larger system via a interface, and it can even be part of a larger scheme that solves the inverse problem, such as the Recursive Greedy Algorithm. This study's results are followed by a discussion on issues related to noise, the precision of the eigenvalue recovery, and possible avenues for adapting this method for a 3D scenario. ViDaExpert is an application for multidimensional data visualization and in-depth analysis, designed to accommodate lists of vectors across various dimensions. The tool offers a range of statistical techniques at its core, allowing for distance measurements, data transformation, classification, and clustering, in addition to SVD and PCA dimensionality reduction methods. With an intuitive graphical interface, users can perform and visualize complex computations, including path integration of trajectories in high-dimensional space, and compare different analysis results side by side. The application is particularly well-suited for biologic sequence analysis and can be run on Linux, macOS, and Windows platforms. The source code for ViDaExpert is available under the BSD license. The application form is downloadable from https://vdaexpert.unicamp.br. The source code is publicly accessible via the GitHub repository at https://github.com/unicamp-vda/vdadot.
